picks.why: The Beam family's label from Clermont, Kentucky, a straight bourbon aged four years and bottled at 80 proof. It is the bourbon a guest names when they mean plain Kentucky bourbon, and the baseline every other pour in the group is tasted against.
picks.note: Confirm the label currently prints Original and the four year statement (one source lists no age). Mash bill of about 77 corn, 13 rye, 10 malted barley is from one source only. Owner is Suntory Global Spirits (formerly Beam Suntory): confirm the current name before printing it. Living Beam family members stay out of prose.

picks.why: The house bourbon of the Frankfort distillery of the same name, released in 1999 when the Sazerac Company renamed the George T. Stagg Distillery. A 90 proof low rye bourbon from the distillery's Mash Bill No. 1, it is the everyday bottle behind Weller, Blanton's, Eagle Rare and the Antique Collection.
picks.note: No age statement; the eight year figure some guides give is unconfirmed. Elmer T. Lee (died 2013) may be named as the master distiller who shaped it. The Antique Collection and Weller bottles on the shelf are this distillery's: link the Library record and the O.F.C. shelf bottle (ofc-2005) from the house page if wanted.

picks.why: The Lawrenceburg, Kentucky bourbon named after a 1940 turkey hunt, owned by the Campari Group since 2009. Its 101 proof flagship is the higher proof, high flavour bourbon a bar reaches for when a cocktail has to stand up to vermouth or citrus.
picks.note: Sources split on the first release, 1940 or 1942: tell it as about 1940 or confirm. Age of six to eight years comes from shop copy only. Its master distillers, father and son, are both living: by role only. Russell's Reserve, a separate label from the same distillery, stands in small-batch-single-barrel.

picks.why: The Brown-Forman bourbon launched in 1996 from its distillery near Versailles, Kentucky. Distiller's Select, 90.4 proof, is a blend of copper pot still whiskey made at Woodford and column still whiskey from Brown-Forman's Louisville plant, which makes it the clear lesson that bourbon need not come from a column still alone.
picks.note: Not on the bourbon benchmarks list; added because it is a Kentucky label guests order by name at nearly every bar. The pot still share (about a fifth, one shop listing) is unconfirmed: do not print a figure. Its master distiller is living: by role only.

picks.why: The Louisville bourbon George Garvin Brown first sold in 1870 in sealed glass bottles, the brand on which Brown-Forman was founded, and sold by the same company before, during and after Prohibition. The 86 Proof, released in 1959, is the bottling that carries that story at the rail.
picks.note: The America's First Bottled Bourbon line is the company's registered claim: say sealed bottles from 1870 and attribute the claim. The Kentucky Historical Society marker dates sealed bottling to the 1870s. Its Whiskey Row distillery is on West Main Street, Louisville. George Garvin Brown (died 1917) may be named.

swaps.why: The owner took Rebel out as a label a fine dining guest does not ask for, and asked for one a guest would; Old Fitzgerald, the historic wheated label of Stitzel-Weller, moves here from bottled-in-bond with its key kept.
The decanter series changes its age with each spring and fall edition; the 7 Year Old, launched in 2025, is the standing bottling a guest can be poured.

picks.why: The Loretto, Kentucky distillery bought in 1953 by Bill Samuels Sr., whose first bourbon was bottled in 1958 with soft red winter wheat in place of rye. At 90 proof, with the red wax dipped neck, it is the wheated bourbon nearly every bar carries and the first one to taste.
picks.note: Mash bill of 70 corn, 16 red winter wheat, 14 malted barley stands on the distillery's own page (the refuted record gives it as the distillery's). Bill Samuels Sr. died in 1992 and may be named; his son and grandson are living: by role only. The Library spells the name with a curly apostrophe; the library field copies it exactly.

picks.why: The wheated bourbon line named for William Larue Weller (1825 to 1899), whose Louisville business dates to 1849, made since 1999 under the Sazerac Company at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort. Special Reserve, 90 proof with no age statement, is the house's everyday bottling and the one on the owner's shelf.
picks.note: Weller is a label of Buffalo Trace, not a distillery: the Library holds no Weller record, link Buffalo Trace. The 1849 wheat recipe claim is the brand's; say the business dates to 1849. Its Stitzel-Weller past is history, told in the past tense. Weller Aged 12 Years (weller-12) is also on the shelf: the second bottle on the house page.

picks.flagship: Pappy Van Winkle's Family Reserve 15 Year Old
picks.why: The Van Winkle family's wheated bourbons, named for Julian "Pappy" Van Winkle (1874 to 1965), who ran the Stitzel-Weller distillery in Louisville from its opening after Prohibition. Made since 2002 by Buffalo Trace to the family's wheated recipe, the 15 Year Old at 107 proof is the bottling a guest means when they ask for Pappy.
picks.note: The owner named this pick. The family's living members (the founder's grandson and great grandson, who run the family company today) must never be named; Julian "Pappy" Van Winkle (1874 to 1965) may be. Stitzel-Weller closed as a bourbon distillery and is told as history in the past tense; confirm whether any 2002 to 2009 bottlings held Stitzel-Weller whiskey before saying so. Confirm that Pappy ran Stitzel-Weller from its opening after Prohibition (the Weller shelf record says so). Keep any talk of once a year release or scarcity out of the prose. Old Rip Van Winkle Distillery is the family company that bottles it: confirm whether the label reads Old Rip Van Winkle Distillery or Buffalo Trace.

picks.flagship: Larceny Small Batch Kentucky Straight Bourbon
picks.why: Heaven Hill's wheated bourbon, distilled at its Bernheim Distillery in Louisville and launched in 2012 and named for John E. Fitzgerald, the bonded warehouse man of the legend told about Old Fitzgerald, its neighbour in this group. At 92 proof with no age statement, it is the wheater a guest is offered when Maker's Mark or Weller is not the answer.
picks.note: Confirm the current label: a recent version reads Larceny Aged 6 Years Small Batch, older ones carry no age. Heaven Hill's claim of a larger wheat share than its nearest rival (25 per cent higher, in its 2024 release) is the producer's: attribute it. Larceny Barrel Proof belongs to this label and is not used in barrel-proof.

picks.why: The historic wheated label of Stitzel-Weller, first sold in 1870 by the brand's account and the distillery's leading bourbon from 1935, made by Heaven Hill at its Bernheim Distillery in Louisville since 1999 from 68 per cent corn, 20 wheat and 12 malted barley. The 7 Year Old Bottled-in-Bond, launched in June 2025 as the label's standing bottling at 100 proof, is the wheater a guest asks for by the Stitzel-Weller name.
picks.note: The owner took Rebel out of this group on 2026-11-22 as a label a fine dining guest does not ask for, and Old Fitzgerald moved here from bottled-in-bond with its key kept. Its flagship moved with it from the twice yearly decanter series (spring and fall editions of differing ages since 2018) to the 7 Year Old, the standing bottling Heaven Hill launched in 2025, because a guest can be poured it at any time of year. Unconfirmed: the exact words the label prints for the age (retail listings read Aged 7 Years), the year the name was first registered (1884 and 1901 both appear on Heaven Hill's pages), and whether every bottle is distilled at Bernheim since Heaven Hill announced a return to distilling in Bardstown in 2022. The bond is the second lesson; wheat is the first.

picks.why: The Lawrenceburg, Kentucky distillery that makes ten bourbon recipes from two mash bills, one of them 35 per cent rye, and five yeasts. Small Batch, 90 proof, blends four of them, two from the high rye bill, and so teaches what rye does to a bourbon better than any single bottle.
picks.note: Owner is Kirin: confirm before printing. Small Batch blends OBSK, OBSO, OESK and OESO, aged six and seven years (the distillery's own Small Batch pages). The yellow label Four Roses Bourbon is the entry bottling; Small Batch was chosen as the one taught. Its master distiller is living: by role only.

picks.why: The Beam family's high rye bourbon label, named for Basil Hayden Sr. and first bottled in 1882, made today at the Jim Beam distillery in Clermont from a mash of about 27 per cent rye. The Bonded bottling, 100 proof, is the version bartenders use for a spirit forward Old Fashioned.
picks.note: Sources split on whether Raymond B. Hayden was a son or grandson and on 1840 or 1882: Beam's own site says first bottled in 1882, use that and leave the lineage line out unless confirmed. The flagship also teaches bottled-in-bond, but the label sits here because its lesson is the rye.

picks.why: Old Grand-Dad's sibling from the same high rye Beam mash, released in 1992 in Beam's Small Batch Bourbon Collection and named for Meredith Basil Hayden Sr. At 80 proof it is the lighter, spicier high rye pour a guest orders by name.
picks.note: The name dropped its possessive (Basil Hayden's) in 2021: use Basil Hayden. Sources give the rye as 27 or 25 per cent: give no figure. Confirm 80 proof on the label, which no search source stated.

picks.why: Diageo's frontier whiskey brand, founded in 1987 and with its own distillery near Shelbyville, Kentucky since 2017, and a mash of 68 per cent corn, 28 per cent rye and 4 per cent malted barley. At 90 proof it is the high rye bourbon found on a great many rails.
picks.note: Not on the high-rye benchmarks list; added because it is the high rye bourbon a working bar is likely to pour. Its founder is living: by role only. Earlier stock was made under contract, much of it at Four Roses until about 2014 (the refuted record); Stitzel-Weller was not confirmed for the standard bourbon: confirm before saying where current bottles are distilled. The 1830 ancestor story is the brand's claim.

picks.why: The Louisville distillery whose Heigold is a high rye, double malted straight bourbon of about 70 corn, 25 malted rye and 5 malted barley, bottled at 95 proof and named for a nineteenth century German stonecutter. It is the owner's shelf bottle and the craft voice of the style.
picks.note: The label's Cavehill (four grain, rabbit-hole-cavehill) is the four-grain-bourbon lesson, left without a group; it can be the second bottle on the house page. Founding year (2012 is widely given) not confirmed by these searches. Its founder is living: by role only.

swaps.why: The owner's instruction to take Rebel out of wheated-bourbon moved Old Fitzgerald there, and New Riff, a bonded bourbon a fine dining guest asks for, takes its place here.

picks.flagship: Colonel E.H. Taylor Small Batch Bottled in Bond
picks.why: Named for Colonel Edmund Haynes Taylor Jr., the Frankfort distiller who fought for the Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 and once owned the distillery now called Buffalo Trace. The Small Batch at 100 proof is the bonded bourbon that carries the law's own history, so the term is the lesson.
picks.note: The term is the lesson in each why here: one distillery, one season, at least four years in a bonded warehouse, 100 proof. Confirm that the label prints Bottled in Bond on the Small Batch. E. H. Taylor died in 1923 and may be named.

picks.flagship: New Riff Bottled in Bond Kentucky Straight Bourbon
picks.why: The Newport, Kentucky distillery across the Ohio River from Cincinnati, opened in 2014, which released no whiskey of its own make until it could be bottled in bond, and whose standard bourbon has carried the bond since its first release in 2018. At least four years old, 100 proof, not chill filtered, from 65 per cent corn, 30 rye and 5 malted barley, it shows the bond as a craft distillery's promise of where and when its whiskey was made.
picks.note: Takes Old Fitzgerald's place here on 2026-11-22, when the owner moved Old Fitzgerald into wheated-bourbon; the lane's alternates were Old Tub and Very Old Barton. The mash bill, the at least four years, the 100 proof and the absence of chill filtration are on the distillery's own pages. The opening in 2014 and the first release of its own bourbon in August 2018 were confirmed by the refuter on 2026-11-22 in two trade accounts (Distillery Trail, The Manual) beside the distillery's story page. The label as the distillery's shop prints it reads New Riff Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey Bottled in Bond: confirm the order of the words on the bottle. Its founder is living: by role only; the name stands in people.json. Earlier the distillery sold a sourced bourbon under another name: history, and not this bottle.

picks.why: Heaven Hill's label, distilled from 1999 at its Bernheim Distillery in Louisville, whose white label Bottled in Bond is a 100 proof straight bourbon aged at least four years in a bonded warehouse. It is the bonded bourbon a bar keeps on the rail, beside the brand's 86 proof Black Label.
picks.note: Placed here rather than in bourbon because its white label is the teaching bottle for the bond; the Black Label is the brand's everyday bourbon. The 2012 introduction of this label form was confirmed by neither the author nor the refuter, and the refuted record gives no year for it. Mash bill 78 corn, 10 rye, 12 malt: written in the record as given, Heaven Hill's traditional recipe, since no Evan Williams page states it.

picks.why: The family owned Bardstown distillery's namesake bourbon, launched in its present form in 2019 at seven years and 100 proof, after a six year bonded bottling sold only in Kentucky ended in 2018. It is the house teaching the bond with an age statement on the label.
picks.note: The name on the label is Heaven Hill Distillery's own: the Library record Heaven Hill links here. The family owners are living: by role only.

picks.flagship: Henry McKenna 10 Year Single Barrel Bottled in Bond
picks.why: Heaven Hill's single barrel label, a bourbon aged ten years and bottled in bond at 100 proof. It pairs the bond with a single barrel and an age statement, so a bartender can teach both terms from one bottle.
picks.note: Not on the benchmarks list; added for its single barrel and age statement. The namesake, Henry McKenna (1819 to 1893), is named with his dates in the refuted record; his death in 1893 rests on secondary accounts.

picks.why: The Buffalo Trace bourbon released in 1984 as a single barrel bourbon, named for Colonel Albert B. Blanton and drawn from Warehouse H at 93 proof. It is the bottle that made single barrel a term guests ask for, and the term is the lesson.
picks.note: Named for Albert B. Blanton (died 1959), who may be named; Elmer T. Lee (died 2013) created it. Mash Bill No. 2 stands on Buffalo Trace's own product page; the refuted record names the bill and gives no percentages and no rye share. Its owner abroad differs by market: keep ownership out.

picks.why: Buffalo Trace's ten year old bourbon, sold as a single barrel from 2005 until the words Single Barrel came off its label about 2012, which shows that a label promises only what it prints. It is the aged bourbon a guest names beside Blanton's.
picks.note: The 90 proof stands on the producer's page; 101 was the Seagram bottling of 1975 to 2005. The label no longer prints Single Barrel, since about 2012 (the refuted record). A swap of the house to Baker's (Baker's Single Barrel 7 Year) was proposed by the author and refused on 2026-11-22: no Baker's record has been written and refuted, and the style's own page names Eagle Rare; the owner may revisit it.

picks.why: Beam's 100 proof small batch bourbon from the Small Batch Bourbon Collection of 1992. Its nine year statement was dropped in 2016 and restored in 2020, which makes it a clear lesson in how age and batch size sit on an American label.
picks.note: Small batch has no legal definition in the United States: say so in the group. Booker Noe (died 2004) created the collection and may be named.

picks.why: Heaven Hill's bourbon named for an eighteenth century Baptist minister, bottled at 94 proof from barrels aged eight to twelve years, without an age statement. It is the small batch bourbon a bar stocks beside Knob Creek.
picks.note: The 1986 first release, as a twelve year old, stands in Heaven Hill's own news and Wikipedia (the refuted record). The minister may be named but the claim that he invented bourbon is a myth to be told as one. Elijah Craig Barrel Proof belongs to this label and is not used in barrel-proof.

picks.why: Wild Turkey's single barrel bourbon, bottled non chill filtered at 110 proof, under a label a son made in 1998 to honour his father, both in their time master distiller at Wild Turkey. It shows how a single barrel from a high proof house reads against the batched Wild Turkey 101.
picks.note: The namesakes, father and son, are both living: never name them, say a father and son who have both been master distiller there. The 110 proof and the non chill filtering stand on the brand's own product page. The 104 proof figure belongs to the Single Barrel Rye, not this.

picks.why: The bourbon Booker Noe, Beam's master distiller, introduced in 1987 by Beam's own pages and on general sale from 1988 by most accounts, straight from the barrel, uncut and unfiltered, aged about six to eight years, at a different natural proof for each batch. It is the barrel proof bourbon by which the term is taught.
picks.note: Booker Noe died in 2004 and may be named; his son and grandson are living: by role only. Proof varies by batch (about 121 to 131 across releases): never print one figure. Placed here, not in small-batch-single-barrel, because uncut is its lesson.

picks.why: The Antique Collection's uncut, unfiltered bourbon from Buffalo Trace, named for the nineteenth century owner of the distillery, released with the Antique Collection in the autumn at its barrel proof. It is the owner's shelf bottle and the aged end of the barrel proof lesson.
picks.note: George T. Stagg (died 1893) may be named. Keep release scarcity out of prose. Proof and age differ by release: print neither as fixed. Stagg's purchase of O.F.C. is 1878 or 1879 by source: the refuted record keeps 1878 in the story and rests no card or question on it.

picks.why: The younger, batched barrel proof bourbon from the same Buffalo Trace recipe as George T. Stagg, sold as Stagg Jr. until it was renamed Stagg in 2022. Uncut and unfiltered, at a proof that changes each batch, it is the shelf bottle that shows barrel proof at a younger age.
picks.note: A separate label on the owner's shelf from George T. Stagg; if the merge agent judges the two one house, keep George T. Stagg and use an alternate. The rename year is 2022 in two sources, not 2023. Merge ruling: the two stand as two labels, each a bottle on the owner's shelf with its own name on the glass. The author tells the namesake's life once, under George T. Stagg, and gives this pick the younger bottling's own story; if the two pages cannot be told apart, the first free alternate of the lane is Penelope.

picks.why: The Sazerac Company's Bardstown bourbon, bottled at 125 proof, the strength at which it entered the barrel, since 2016. It teaches the difference between barrel entry proof and barrel proof, a distinction the term depends on.
picks.note: Reviewers say it is not quite cask strength: the lesson is that it is cut back to its entry proof. Age (about 8.5 years in the launch release) is not on the label. Plain slug 1792; the label reads 1792 Bourbon.

picks.why: The Louisville independent blender that buys aged straight bourbon from Indiana, Tennessee and Kentucky and bottles each numbered batch at cask strength, non chill filtered. It shows barrel proof as a blender's choice rather than a distiller's.
picks.note: The founding year, 2013, stands on the house's own About page and a trade release (the refuted record). Each batch has its own number, proof and sources: teach the series, not a batch. Its founder is living: by role only.

swaps.why: The house renamed No. 12 Signature Recipe on its labels and its own pages, the whisky unchanged at 90 proof; the record was written for it and refuted.

picks.why: The Lynchburg, Tennessee distillery whose whiskey passes through sugar maple charcoal before the barrel, the Lincoln County Process it calls charcoal mellowing. Old No. 7 is the bottle a guest pictures at the words Tennessee whiskey.
picks.note: Nearest Green, the enslaved and later freed distiller who taught Jasper Newton Daniel, may be named (both long dead); his role is told by the brand and by historians. The 1866 registration date was not confirmed by these searches: leave it out or confirm. Settled by the refuted record: 1866 is told as the house's own date beside a biographer's 1875 from the deed records, and year is left empty. Proof differs by market (80 in the United States).

picks.why: The Cascade Hollow distillery near Tullahoma, in Coffee County, Tennessee, built from 1958 in the hollow where the first Cascade distillery stood from the late 1870s, which chills its whiskey before the charcoal. Signature Recipe, sold until its rename as No. 12, is the classic Dickel bottling and the clear contrast with Jack Daniel's.
picks.note: Owner is Diageo: confirm. Proof of No. 12 (90) not stated by these searches: confirm. Settled: 90 proof on the house's listing and in Distiller. The bottling swap from No. 12 to Signature Recipe was agreed by the refuter on 22 November 2026; the year of the rename was not found. Dickel spells whisky without the e: keep the label's spelling. George Dickel (died 1894) may be named.

picks.why: The Shelbyville, Tennessee brand named for Nathan "Nearest" Green, who taught Jack Daniel to distil. Its 1856 bottling is a 100 proof Tennessee whiskey passed through the Lincoln County Process.
picks.note: Its founder is living: by role only. The 1856 date is the brand's belief from its own research, not settled fact: say so. Early bottles were sourced; two trade accounts say the 1856 moved to whiskey the brand made itself in 2022, and where that whiskey is distilled is not settled. The label adds a further descriptive word after 1856 that house voice forbids: keep it out of prose.

picks.why: The Nashville distillery revived in 2014 by descendants of Charles Nelson, whose family's Green Brier distillery ran until Tennessee's prohibition shut it in 1909. Its Tennessee whiskey is wheated, mellowed through sugar maple charcoal and bottled at 91 proof.
picks.note: The founders are living descendants: by role only. Charles Nelson and Louisa Nelson (both nineteenth century) may be named. The old distillery is history in the past tense. Its Belle Meade bourbon is the house's other label, not this flagship.

picks.why: The Kelso, Tennessee distillery founded in 1997 and housed in an old schoolhouse, which makes its whiskey in pot stills and is the one Tennessee producer the state law of 2013 lets call it Tennessee whiskey without the charcoal step, an exception the attorney general's opinion of 2015 judged likely unconstitutional. It is the exception that proves the rule.
picks.note: Its founder is living: by role only. Sources split on 1997 or 1999 for the first distillation; the record gives 1997 as the founding and tells both years for the schoolhouse. Benjamin Prichard is a historic ancestor and may be named once his dates are confirmed. A second distillery opened in Nashville in May 2014, on the grounds of the Fontanel Mansion; whether it still runs was not found.

picks.flagship: Rittenhouse Straight Rye Whisky Bottled in Bond
picks.why: A Philadelphia rye name, first sold by Continental Distilling, that Heaven Hill took over in 1993 by its own history (1999 in VinePair and The Whiskey Wash) and has made in Kentucky since. The bonded bottling is the one to know: four years old, 100 proof, from a mash at the legal minimum of 51 per cent rye, which is the Kentucky way with rye and the bar's working rye for a Manhattan or a Sazerac.
picks.note: Sources differ on the mash: 51 rye, 35 corn, 14 malted barley on Heaven Hill linked sheets, 51, 37, 12 in several reviews; confirm on Heaven Hill's own sheet. Settled: 51, 35 and 14 is the house's own figure for its rye recipe, and the record gives it so. Heaven Hill's claim that it follows a Pennsylvania style is disputed; keep it out of the why. The bonded label also fits the bottled-in-bond group in the other American lane; it is placed here because a bartender reaches for it as a rye. Library holds the maker, Heaven Hill, not the label.

picks.why: The Sazerac Company's own rye, named for the New Orleans cocktail and distilled at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort from a rye mash the trade puts a little over the 51 per cent line (low rye is the name of Buffalo Trace's bourbon mash, not this one). Bottled at 90 proof, it is the rye that the Sazerac cocktail is now built on by name.
picks.note: The label carries no age statement; it is widely said to be about six years old and some retail copy still says 6 Year, but this is not on the label: leave it out or give it as a belief. The mash bill is not published. A 100 proof bottling was added in 2025 and an 18 year release exists; neither is the flagship. Library holds the maker, Buffalo Trace.

picks.flagship: Thomas H. Handy Sazerac Straight Rye
picks.why: The rye of the Buffalo Trace Antique Collection, released once a year uncut and unfiltered at barrel proof and named for Thomas H. Handy, the clerk who with fellow employees bought the Sazerac House in New Orleans in 1869, by the company's account, and from whose firm the Sazerac Company grew. It is Sazerac Rye's mash at full strength, the bottle on the owner's own shelf.
picks.note: Proof moves by release (about 126 in 2016, about 130 in 2025). Maxim reports that from the 2026 release every barrel is at least 12 years old, against about six years before; only one source, so confirm on Buffalo Trace's 2026 release before stating an age. Settled: Whisky Advocate, The Whiskey Wash and the distillery's press release give the twelve year floor from the release of 2026. It also suits the barrel-proof group in the other American lane; placed here as a rye, and it is a shelf bottle.

picks.why: A Maryland rye name from 1895, made in Maryland until distilling there ended (1972 in secondary accounts, the 1980s in Heaven Hill's) and in Kentucky by Heaven Hill, which bought it in 1982; the six year old 110 proof bottling of 2015 is the one to know. It teaches how a Maryland name came to stand for a Kentucky rye.
picks.note: Sources disagree on when Heaven Hill took the brand (1982 in one, the 1980s in Heaven Hill's release) and on the mash (51 rye, 39 corn, 10 barley against 65, 23, 12): confirm on Heaven Hill's sheet. Settled in part: Heaven Hill's Pikesville page gives 1982; its own pages give the mash two ways (51, 39 and 10, or 51, 35 and 14), and 65, 23, 12 appears on none, so the record promises only the 51 per cent rye. Made at the Bernheim Distillery, by the house's 2015 launch release. The older 80 proof three year Pikesville is still sold in Maryland; do not confuse the two. Could be told under monongahela-rye as history; placed here because the whiskey is Kentucky made, as the benchmarks place it.

picks.flagship: Michter's US*1 Single Barrel Kentucky Straight Rye
picks.why: A Louisville house whose name goes back to a Pennsylvania distillery, and whose US*1 rye is bottled one barrel at a time at 84.8 proof. It is the rye a guest asks for by the Michter's name, gentler in proof than the bonded ryes.
picks.note: Michter's also sells a US*1 bourbon; if the other American lane claims Michter's as a bourbon label, drop this pick for an alternate. Sources differ on where it is distilled (Shively or Fort Nelson in Louisville, and older reviews call it sourced): say Louisville, Kentucky only until Michter's own page settles it. Settled: by Michter's own Shively page it bought the building in 2011 and first filled barrels there in August 2015; earlier bottlings were distilled for it by others. Mash bill (53, 33, 14 per one retailer) unconfirmed. The Library spells the name with a curly apostrophe; the library field copies it exactly. Merge ruling: the bourbon lane holds Michter's only as an alternate, so the pick stands here.

swaps.why: The house's own shop names its straight rye Wigle Reserve Pennsylvania Straight Rye; the older name has gone, and the record was written for the Reserve and refuted.

picks.why: The Overholt family's rye from West Overton in Pennsylvania, first distilled in 1810, and the name that carries the Monongahela story to the bar. Today it is a four year old straight rye at 86 proof, made in Kentucky.
picks.note: Tell the Pennsylvania distilling as history in the past tense: Beam bought the brand in 1987 and makes it in Kentucky; the Oxford Companion has the whiskey already at Forks of Elkhorn near Frankfort before 1987 and one trade source dates a move to 1993, so the record names no distillery and no year for the move. The rise to 86 proof without chill filtering came in 2020 and the fourth year in 2022 (two trade accounts), not together in 2019. A bonded bottling from 2018 exists. Library holds the maker as Jim Beam.

picks.why: The Baltimore distillery that brought Maryland rye back to the bar. Its Signature Rye blends two straight rye mash bills, one high in rye for spice and one lower for sweetness, at 83 proof.
picks.note: Sources say earlier batches were sourced from MGP in Indiana; the house gives Small Batch, of May 2024, as its first rye made wholly in Maryland. Confirm what the current Signature batch is before calling it Maryland distilled. Four to six years is the house's age for Small Batch, not the Signature; one source gives the Signature two years, and the record gives no age. Founding year not confirmed in this run. The author's proposed bottling swap to Sagamore Small Batch Rye Whiskey was refused on 22 November 2026: the record stands written and refuted for the Signature, and a swap needs the record rewritten for Small Batch and refuted first; the house's spirits list omits the Signature while a Signature page stands.

picks.why: A distillery a family opened in Pittsburgh's Strip District in March 2012 to revive Monongahela rye, milling, fermenting and pot distilling regional grain itself; in August 2022 the family agreed to sell it to Pittsburgh Spirits. Its Reserve straight rye is the bottling that shows the western Pennsylvania style at the bar.
picks.note: No source settled a single core bottling or its proof (47.2, 50.5 and 100 proof listed for different rye bottlings; a single barrel rye at 68 rye, 18 wheat, 14 barley). Confirm the current core rye and its label name on Wigle's own site. Founding year not confirmed (2011 assumed, not found); the record gives the opening to the public in March 2012 and leaves year empty. Corporate name differs between sources, and Pittsburgh Distilling Company was not confirmed after the 2022 sale.

picks.why: Made in Bristol, Pennsylvania, since 2011 from a mash of 80 per cent rye with malted barley and malted rye and no corn, in the pure rye way of old Monongahela. The classic bottling, aged in quarter casks and bottled at 90 proof, is the one to know.
picks.note: A living co founder is named in the press; keep him out of prose. Latest confirmation it is operating is a 2024 profile; check it is still open. The bonded bottling is listed at 95 and 100 proof by different sellers; bonded must be 100, so confirm. The classic's age (about eight and a half months in quarter casks) is from one older source; the house says at least six months, which the record keeps. The 95 proof listing belongs to the house's straight rye, not the bonded one.

picks.why: A Washington, Pennsylvania distillery carrying the old Monongahela tradition forward with a high rye mash. Its Old Monongahela rye, bottled at its 108 barrel entry proof, puts the style's name on the label.
picks.note: Introduced in 2024 (May in two trade posts, July in one) and sold in batches, though the house bottles at the barrel entry proof of 108; a 92 proof straight rye is also made and may suit as the everyday flagship: author to choose. Some reviews misspell the maker as Mango Creek. Not on the benchmarks list.

picks.why: A Seattle distillery founded in 2010 or 2011 by the accounts, whose American Oak, first released in 2013, was its flagship until the house ceased making it and put Westland Flagship in its place: five malts of barley matured predominantly in new American oak, by the house's account, and bottled at 46 per cent. It is the bottle that shows what the new category tastes like.
picks.note: Maturation differs by source (at least 24 months against 40 months for another Westland malt); the 40 months belongs to Westland Flagship, and the house gives no figure for American Oak. Its parent company was not confirmed in this run; leave ownership out. Swap to Westland Flagship refused at the read together of 22 November 2026: the record was written and refuted for American Oak and tells its end truly, and a record for Flagship (key and card ids five-malts and successor kept) would need its own author and refuter.

picks.flagship: Stranahan's Original American Single Malt Whiskey
picks.why: A Denver distillery founded in 2004 whose Original, first bottled in 2006 by one account, is aged in new American oak with a number 3 char (at least four years on the house's shop page, six to nine on its main page) and bottled at 94 proof. It is the Colorado malt a guest asks for by name.
picks.note: Proximo Spirits bought it in 2010 (Westword, Wikipedia; 2011 in one account). The six to nine years stands on the house's own main page beside the four year minimum of its shop, so the record gives both as the house's and no single figure. Older labels read Stranahan's Colorado Whiskey; confirm the label name today.

picks.why: Clear Creek's peated malt from Oregon, released in 1996 by its founder Steve McCarthy (a first distillation of 1991 rests on Whisky Advocate alone and is left out), years before American single malt was a term. It teaches where the category came from.
picks.note: Steve McCarthy died on 2 January 2023, so he may be named. Clear Creek was sold to Hood River Distillers in 2014, and in 2017 Hood River Distillers announced the move of its work from Portland to Hood River. The bottling is three years in air-dried Oregon oak at 85 proof; McCarthy's 6 Year Oregon Single Malt, at 100 proof, is a separate release.

picks.why: A Portland, Oregon malt brewed and distilled from Northwest two row barley and aged in new American oak, heavily toasted and lightly charred, bottled at 90 proof. It is the original Westward bottling, with stout cask and cask strength versions beside it.
picks.note: Its master distiller is living; keep him out of prose. Ownership not confirmed (no source named Diageo); leave it out. The house's product page names the bottling Westward Whiskey Original; whether the label reads so was not seen, a question of name only, and no swap was proposed. House Spirits filed for Chapter 11 in April 2025 and a court approved the sale of most of its assets in October 2025; the closing was not confirmed.

picks.flagship: Courage & Conviction American Single Malt Whisky
picks.why: A Lovingston, Virginia distillery given over to single malt, whose flagship of 2020 is distilled on site from malted barley, aged at least three years by the house's landing page and four by its shop, and bottled at 46 per cent. It shows the category reaching the East.
picks.note: One source calls it the largest dedicated American single malt distillery; keep that out. Its founder, Dr. George G. Moore, has died (2013 in one account and one page of dates, not two sources), so the record keeps him by role. The house's pages call the bottling Courage & Conviction Signature Malt, while the Virginia ABC listing and the house's shop keep American Single Malt Whisky. Swap to Signature Malt refused at the read together of 22 November 2026: no label was seen, and the record, refuted for the roster's words, gives the other name in its traps.

picks.flagship: Mellow Corn Bottled in Bond Kentucky Straight Corn Whiskey
picks.why: Heaven Hill's corn whiskey, bonded: at least four years in a bonded warehouse and 100 proof, from a mash Heaven Hill states only as at least 80 per cent corn (given as 80 per cent corn, 12 malted barley and 8 rye; some listings give about 90). It is the aged corn whiskey a bar carries, and the clearest bottle for the rule that corn whiskey goes into used or uncharred oak.
picks.note: The used or uncharred oak rule is the style's own, from the Cask Atlas; not searched in this run. The 90 per cent is a retailer's share; Tasting Table and Heaven Hill's 2023 Heritage Collection release give 80, 12 and 8. Also bonded, but placed here because the lesson is corn.

picks.why: A corn whiskey in a mason jar, made in Kentucky by Heaven Hill from at least 80 per cent corn, the legal floor (81 per cent by retailers quoting its sheet), and bottled at 80 proof, with "less than 30 days old" on its label. It shows the young, near clear end of the style.
picks.note: Some sources call it unaged and the maker's sheet says lightly aged; quote the label's own words. The sheet that says lightly aged was not found; Heaven Hill's own writing calls it unaged. A 100 proof Fruit Jar version exists. The two flavoured jars of 2008 were Peach and Lemonade, at 70 proof.

picks.why: A Gatlinburg, Tennessee distillery opened in 2010 whose Original is unaged corn whiskey by its producer's page (corn whiskey on the jar in retail listings, Tennessee Corn Whiskey in one): clear and 100 proof from at least 80 per cent corn, the rest of the recipe unpublished. It is the moonshine a guest names, and it teaches that legal moonshine is corn whiskey with no oak.
picks.note: The licensing milestone is told differently by source (first federally licensed in East Tennessee, or first under the new state law); leave it out or confirm. The legal class on the label (corn whiskey) is from retail label images; confirm on the label itself.

picks.why: A straight corn whiskey sold in a cork-sealed ceramic jug at 80 proof by McCormick Distilling, with no age stated on the producer's pages (three years or 30 months in shop listings only). It is the jug a guest remembers, and an aged corn beside the young ones.
picks.note: Age given as 36 months by most and 30 months by one seller; the older 100 proof bottling is no longer listed. Where McCormick distils it was not confirmed; say bottled by McCormick unless confirmed.

picks.why: Waco's first whisky, launched in 2009 from roasted heirloom blue corn and aged in used oak casks by the producer's account, at 92 proof (distilled twice and small barrels were found in no source). It shows a craft corn whisky built to be sipped, and it is spelt whisky on the label.
picks.note: First Texas whisky since Prohibition is the brand's own claim; keep it out of the why unless a second source confirms it. The corn began as Hopi blue corn from New Mexico by Imbibe's account (Arizona in one other) before a blue flint corn grown in West Texas; the producer's page says 100 per cent blue corn, grown in Texas and roasted.

picks.flagship: Monkey Shoulder Blended Malt Scotch Whisky
picks.why: William Grant & Sons' blended malt of Speyside malts, first from Glenfiddich, The Balvenie and Kininvie, launched in the early 2000s and named for the strained shoulder of the maltmen who turned barley by hand. It was made to mix, and it is the bottle that taught bars the words blended malt.
picks.note: Launch year 2003 by some sources, 2005 by others: settled as the release in Britain and France in 2005 (The Spirits Business, The Whiskey Wash), with 2003 as the start of work by one account. Batch 27 on the collar is said to mean batches of 27 casks by one source only. Strength 40% ABV in Britain and 43% ABV in a United States listing: confirm by market. The current malt make up is not published; tell the three distilleries as its origin.

picks.why: The London blending house founded in 2000, which distils nothing and builds its whiskies from bought casks, and which pressed the trade to let a label say what is in the bottle. The Peat Monster, a blended malt of Islay and Highland malts at 46% ABV, is its long running core bottling and the clearest lesson in how a blender handles smoke.
picks.note: The Spice Tree (2005) is the story of the inner staves the Scotch Whisky Association objected to, but Decanter reports it has been axed from the range: tell it as history. The Penicillin was first made with Compass Box Asyla, a blended Scotch now gone. The founder is living: describe him by role. Confirm The Peat Monster is still listed on the house pages.

picks.why: The Glasgow bottlers Douglas Laing & Co. released Big Peat in 2009 as the first of their Remarkable Regional Malts: a blended malt of Islay malts including Ardbeg, Bowmore, Caol Ila and Port Ellen, closed in 1983 and reopened in March 2024, at 46% ABV without chill filtering or colour. It is the bottle to know for Islay smoke without a single distillery's name on it.
picks.note: Port Ellen in the mix is from the label and retailers; Port Ellen was closed for decades and has since been rebuilt: confirm the reopening year and what the current batches hold, and tell its share as history. The family running Douglas Laing are living: keep them out.

picks.why: A blended malt finished in first fill Oloroso sherry casks, sold as Naked Grouse until 2021 when it was renamed Naked Malt with the recipe unchanged. It is the sherried blended malt a bar meets on the rail, the contrast to the bourbon cask Monkey Shoulder.
picks.note: Strength 40% ABV by the rename coverage, 43% ABV by one 2018 review: confirm by market. The rename coverage of 2021 names The Macallan, Highland Park and The Glenrothes as its malts, and a trade report of 2017 adds Glenturret. Edrington agreed in September 2024 to sell The Famous Grouse and Naked Malt to William Grant & Sons, and the sale was completed on 1 July 2025 (Edrington, William Grant, The Drinks Business, Whisky Magazine): madeBy moved from Edrington to William Grant & Sons at the read together of 22 November 2026, with the refuter's agreement, and the record tells the sale only as dated history.

picks.why: A blended malt of Highland malts at 40% ABV, built on the replica of the Mackinlay's Rare Old Highland Malt that Ernest Shackleton took to Antarctica in 1907, whose crates were lifted from beneath his hut at Cape Royds in January 2010 by the Antarctic Heritage Trust's account (first seen there in 2006 or 2007 by others). It is the bottle that carries the story of how a blender reads an old whisky and remakes it.
picks.note: The replica of 2011 (47.3% ABV) and this later blended malt are two bottlings: keep them apart. The blender who made the replica is living: describe him by role. The original was distilled at Glen Mhor, closed in the 1980s: told as history. Confirm the current label name.

picks.flagship: Johnnie Walker Black Label 12 Year Old
picks.why: The Kilmarnock house that grew from the grocery John Walker opened in 1820; his son Alexander made its first commercial blend, Old Highland Whisky, in the 1860s. Its aged blend, Extra Special Old Highland Whisky, was renamed Black Label in 1909, and it is the aged blend a bar pours when a guest asks for Scotch by a label, the yardstick for every blend that follows.
picks.note: Sources split on the first blend, 1865 or 1867 for registration: tell it as the 1860s. Diageo makes it today; say no more of ownership. Green Label, the blended malt, belongs to this label and is held here, not in the blended malt group. The strength is 40% ABV on the house's British pages and 43% on its South African page, so the refuted record says 43% in some markets. Whisky Magazine has the 12 Years Old statement come soon after the relaunch of 1906, so the twelve years are not dated to the start of the blend.

picks.why: The Aberdeen blend of Chivas Brothers, merchants since the early nineteenth century; Chivas Regal was first, by the house's account, a 25 year old blend of 1909, and the twelve year old followed in 1938, again by its account. Its heart is Strathisla malt from Keith, and it is the rounder, honeyed Speyside blend to set beside Johnnie Walker.
picks.note: Sources split on the twelve year old, 1938 or a 1939 United States release: tell it as the late 1930s. The blender of 1909 is not named: the refuted record found a Charles Howard named beside another blender and no dates for either. 1801 is the house's year for the Aberdeen grocery, later on King Street, not for the whisky; whether the label prints Established 1801 Aberdeen was not confirmed. Seagram bought the Milton distillery at Keith in 1950, renamed Strathisla in 1951. The Chivas name also stands in the mizunara benchmarks; keep the group here.

picks.why: John Dewar opened his wine and spirits shop in Perth in 1846; White Label was blended in 1899 by the firm's first master blender from outside the family, with Aberfeldy malt at its heart. It is the blend a bartender reaches for when a guest wants Scotch long, with soda or ginger ale.
picks.note: Aberfeldy was building from 1896 and distilling from 1898 (the house and Whisky Magazine, in the refuted record). A. J. Cameron is not named: no two sources gave his death, and the house dates his first creation to 1897. The core White Label carries no age statement.

picks.why: The Perth blend that Matthew Gloag & Son first sold in the late 1890s as The Grouse Brand and named The Famous Grouse on 12 August 1905, by the house's account, its red grouse drawn by the daughter of the founder's grandson. It is the everyday blend to know from Perth, tied to the Glenturret distillery, which once housed The Famous Grouse Experience and gave a peated malt to Smoky Black in 2015.
picks.note: The Grouse Brand is dated 1896 or 1897 by source, so the record says the late 1890s; the malt make up is not published; any malt named in prose needs two sources. Edrington agreed in September 2024 to sell The Famous Grouse and Naked Malt to William Grant & Sons, and the sale was completed in July 2025 (the author's report: The Grocer, Whisky Magazine, Whisky Advocate, Edrington's own release): madeBy moved from Matthew Gloag & Son to William Grant & Sons at the read together of 22 November 2026, as for Naked Malt, the refuter having left the ruling to it, and the record tells only the sale of 1970. British grocers list the core bottle as The Famous Grouse Finest; Finest is not in the flagship, so it stays off the label terms, and the refuter refused a bottling swap for it. The word Famous is the label's name, never a claim.

picks.why: George Ballantine opened a grocery in the Cowgate of Edinburgh in 1827 and moved the business to Glasgow in the 1860s; Ballantine's Finest came in 1910 and has been the house's standard blend ever since. It is the lighter house blend to set beside Johnnie Walker and Chivas Regal when a drink calls for a mixing Scotch.
picks.note: Finest is the label's own word and will trip the superlative lint in prose; quote it only as the name. Sources give 1865 or 1869 for Glasgow, and 40 or about 50 component whiskies: keep counts out. No confirmed Glenburgie link to Finest; leave it out. George Ballantine (1809 to 1891) may be named: two sources agree on his death and the house gives his birth (the refuted record). Hiram Walker's purchase is dated 1935, 1936 or 1937 by source and stays undated; the Dumbarton grain distillery, completed in 1938, was mothballed in 2002, so nothing about Dumbarton is told as present.

picks.why: The family distillery William Grant built in Dufftown, whose first spirit ran on Christmas Day 1887. The 12 Year Old, at 40% ABV, marries Oloroso sherry and bourbon casks in oak tuns, and it is a single malt a guest new to Scotch will often name.
picks.note: The producer's own pages head the bottling 12 Year Old Our Original Twelve, which settles the label words (the refuted record). The 2000 change from a non age statement bottling rests on one reference source and is left out. William Grant is dated 1839 to 1923 by Wikipedia and the producer's timeline. Library holds Glenfiddich.

picks.why: George Smith took out a licence for his still in the glen of the Livet in 1824, after the Excise Act of 1823 made legal distilling worth doing, and the distillery has worked almost without a break since. The 12 Year Old, matured in European and then American oak and bottled at 40% ABV, is the soft, fruity Speyside benchmark.
picks.note: Keep the licence claim narrow: the producer says the first legal licence in the parish of Glenlivet; some sources say the first in Speyside or in Scotland, which is not agreed. Double Oak stands on the 12's label in Britain as in the United States (the producer's British page and Difford's Guide), so the refuted record prints it as a label term for every market. Library holds no Glenlivet record.

picks.flagship: The Macallan Sherry Oak 12 Years Old
picks.why: The Craigellachie distillery dated to 1824 whose house style is built on oak casks seasoned with sherry in Jerez. Sherry Oak 12, at 40% ABV and 43% in some markets, is the bottling that teaches what sherry seasoned oak does to a Speyside malt: dried fruit, spice and a deep colour from the wood alone.
picks.note: The producer says predominantly sherry seasoned European oak; some retailers say exclusively, so do not write exclusively. Double Cask 12 (European and American sherry seasoned oak, 40%, launched 2016) is the more common bar bottle in some markets; the refuter refused a swap to it, as Sherry Oak 12 teaches sherry seasoned oak, and the record gives Double Cask under others. Library holds The Macallan.

picks.why: The second distillery William Grant built in Dufftown, begun in 1892 in Balvenie New House beside Glenfiddich, with its first spirit on 1 May 1893. DoubleWood, launched in 1993, spends twelve years in American oak and then nine months in European oak sherry casks, so it is the bottling that teaches what a cask finish is, at 40% ABV in Britain and 43% in the United States.
picks.note: The producer's own page gives European oak sherry casks for the finish, and the nine months after twelve years in American oak (the refuted record). No source read places the distillery beside Balvenie Castle, so the castle is left out. The floor maltings and coppersmiths are in the record; whether the distillery keeps its own cooperage was not settled.

picks.why: A Speyside distillery in the village of Aberlour, rebuilt by James Fleming in 1879, whose A'bunadh, in its numbered batches, is matured in Spanish oak butts that held Oloroso sherry and bottled at cask strength with no age statement, each batch numbered. It is the bottling that teaches cask strength in a sherried Speysider.
picks.note: Strength moves by batch, about 59 to 62% ABV; never print one figure. The founding year is disputed: 1879 under Fleming, or 1826 for an earlier distillery on the site; tell both or neither. Whether the casks are all first fill differs by source. A bar more often carries Aberlour 12 Year Old or 16 Year Old Double Cask Matured; the refuter refused a swap to the 12 Year Old Double Cask, as the A'bunadh Sherry Cask Collection of October 2025, finished in Oloroso and Pedro Ximenez casks, is a separate series and the numbered batches run on unchanged.

picks.why: A distillery at Tain on the Dornoch Firth, founded in 1843, whose stills have necks over five metres high, which gives a light, floral spirit. The Original, twelve years in ex bourbon American oak since July 2024 and ten before, at 40% ABV, is the clean Highland malt and the reference for what bourbon casks alone give.
picks.note: Since July 2024 the label states 12 Years Old (the producer, Drinks Intel, Whisky Magazine), and the record prints Glenmorangie The Original 12 Years Old; every word of the flagship stands on the new label, so no swap. Keep the stills as a measured fact (5.14 m necks per the owner group), not a ranking.

picks.why: A small distillery in the middle of the West Highland port of Oban, where brothers of the local Stevenson family began distilling in 1794 and the town grew up around the distillery. The 14 Year Old, at 43% ABV, became its West Highland entry in the Classic Malts, and it is the coastal Highland malt a guest asks for by name.
picks.note: The Classic Malts launch is given as 1987, 1988 or 1989 by different sources; leave the year out. The founders' names are given as John and Hugh Stevenson, sometimes with James, so the record says brothers and names neither; the family held it until 1866, and the buyer of 1883 rebuilt it in the years after (1883 to 1887 in one account, 1890 to 1894 in others).

picks.why: A distillery at Alness on the Cromarty Firth, founded by Alexander Matheson in 1839 and later run by the Mackenzies, whose clan stag is on every bottle. The 12 Year Old starts in American white oak casks that held bourbon, and a portion then moves to Oloroso sherry casks, at 40% ABV: the rich, sherried Highland malt.
picks.note: The stag came with the Mackenzies, who took over the running in 1867 and bought the distillery from the founder's son in 1891 (the refuted record); the year it first reached a label is not settled. The producer says only that some of the sherry casks held aged Oloroso, so no bodega is named for the 12; the Matusalem casks belong to the Cigar Malt Reserve. Sherry Cask Select is a separate 12 at a higher strength; do not confuse them.

picks.why: A distillery more than a thousand feet up in the Central Highlands (sources give 1,070 to 1,164 feet), built in 1897 with spirit first run in 1898, in the pass on the road from Perth to Inverness. The 15 Year Old, at 43% ABV, is the bottling a guest will meet: a gentle, honeyed Highland malt that a guest who wants no smoke will often name.
picks.note: Not in the style's benchmarks today; chosen over Glengoyne and Edradour because it is a Classic Malt a working bar is likelier to carry. The altitude claim varies (highest or second highest working distillery, depending on Braeval); keep to more than a thousand feet and avoid a ranking. No producer page read ties the 15 to the Classic Malts, whose year is given as 1987 or 1989, so the record leaves them out.

picks.why: A distillery at Brora in Sutherland, built in 1967 and 1968 beside the site first worked in 1819, whose spirit is known for a waxy texture and goes largely into Johnnie Walker blends. The 14 Year Old, at 46% ABV, is the malt that teaches texture as a distillery character.
picks.note: The share that goes to Johnnie Walker (about 95%) rests on one source; leave the figure out or confirm. The old distillery became Brora; the renaming year differs by source. Some old listings give 43%; the producer's page gives 46%. The official 14's year of 2002 rests on shops and a review site only and is left out (the refuted record).

picks.why: The distillery at Carbost on Loch Harport, Isle of Skye, founded in 1830 by two brothers who had come from Eigg, the MacAskills, with a lease from the MacLeods. The 10 Year Old, bottled at 45.8% ABV, is peppery, smoky and maritime, and it is the island malt that sits between Islay smoke and Highland sweetness.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: Wikipedia and Difford's give 1830 for the founding by both brothers, with 1831 for the opening at Carbost after the lease; no two sources give either brother's death, so the record names neither in full. The Ledger's islands style names Hugh and Kenneth MacAskill in a quiz stem with no dates, for the integrator. The Islands are not a protected region: in law these distilleries are Highland, as the record's class and first trap say.

picks.flagship: Highland Park 12 Year Old Viking Honour
picks.why: The distillery at Kirkwall on Orkney, dated by the house to 1798 and to a church beadle of its legend, which turns about a fifth of its malt by hand on its own floors and dries it over peat cut on Hobbister Moor, made largely of heather. The 12 Year Old Viking Honour, mostly from sherry seasoned European and American oak at 40% ABV, is the honeyed, gently smoky island malt.
picks.note: The 1798 link is told as the brand's legend, as asked; the beadle and the farmer of High Park are described and not named, since no two sources give their dates (and a living Eunson stands in people.json). The floor share is settled at about a fifth (a trade guide and Whisky Magazine). Viking Honour is the 2017 name of the 12, the whisky unchanged. Library holds Highland Park; its line on Orkney's wind and even temperature is taken only as the house's claim of less spirit lost, for the integrator.

picks.why: The one whisky distillery on the Isle of Jura, at Craighouse: founded in 1810, closed in 1901, and rebuilt from 1960 by two landowners of the island who wanted work for islanders, reopening in 1963 with tall stills. The 12 Year Old, twelve years in American white oak ex-bourbon casks at 40% ABV by the producer's page, took the place of the 10 Year Old in 2025 as the gentle island malt, peach, citrus and walnut rather than smoke; the 10, finished in Oloroso sherry casks, is now its history.
picks.note: Flagship moved from Jura 10 Year Old to Jura 12 Year Old on 2026-11-23: the house announced in August 2025 that the 12 replaces the 10 at the head of its age-stated range, on British shelves from October 2025 and abroad after, and the producer's pages list the 12 at 40% ABV. The record was rewritten for the 12, keeping the key and the card ids sherry-finish and rebuilt, and awaits a refuter. Open: launch coverage gives the 12 an Oloroso finish while the producer's page names only ex-bourbon casks; the back label should settle it. The producer's pages print Jura, not Isle of Jura. Whyte and Mackay bought the distillery in the early 1990s (1993 or 1994 by source); the record tells it as history.

picks.why: Arran's single malt has been made at Lochranza in the north of the island since 1995, when spirit first ran on 29 June; a second distillery opened at Lagg in the south in 2019, and that year the Lochranza Distillery name went onto the Arran label. The 10 Year Old, mainly bourbon casks with a portion finished in first-fill Oloroso sherry casks, at 46% ABV, non chill filtered and of natural colour, is the unpeated island malt.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: first spirit on 29 June and the official opening on 17 August 1995 (the producer and Wikipedia), and the casks on the producer's page. No source shows a renaming of the first distillery, only the Lochranza Distillery name on the label from 2019. Machrie Moor, Lochranza's peated label, and Lagg's own label stand only among the record's other bottlings, never as this pick. The founder, dead by one source, is described and not named.

picks.why: The one distillery on the Isle of Mull, in the harbour town of Tobermory, dated by the house to 1798 and first called Ledaig. It sells its unpeated malt as Tobermory and its peated malt as Ledaig; the 12 Year Old, launched when the distillery reopened in 2019 after two years closed for refurbishment, twelve years in American oak at 46.3% ABV, is the unpeated house style.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the 12 replaced the 10 at the 2019 reopening (The Spirits Business, Scottish Field) and stands in the producer's core range; 1798 is on the producer's story page and in Wikipedia. The founder, a merchant of the town, is described, as no dates were found. Ledaig 10 Year Old stands only among the record's other bottlings, since both are one distillery.

picks.why: A distillery at Clydebank on the edge of Glasgow, licensed in 1823, that distils all of its spirit three times, a habit once shared by other Lowland houses, which gives a light, clean malt. The 12 Year Old, relabelled 12 Year Old Double Cask in 2025 and matured in American oak bourbon casks and Spanish oak Oloroso sherry casks at 40% ABV, is a Lowland malt a guest will often meet.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: 1823 and Clydebank (Difford's Guide, Wikipedia, the producer's history). The ranking of retail copy is kept out; the record keeps to what the house does. In 2025 the house put out the 12 Year Old Double Cask in place of its 12 Year Old; the record prints Auchentoshan 12 Year Old Double Cask Single Malt Scotch Whisky, which carries every word of the flagship, so no swap was made, as for Glenmorangie The Original. The integrator may write the flagship as Auchentoshan 12 Year Old Double Cask by an agreed bottling swap, the key and card ids kept.

picks.why: A distillery at Pencaitland in East Lothian, near Edinburgh, begun, by the account most often told, as Milton by two brothers of the Rate family about 1825 and licensed as Glenkinchie in 1837. The 12 Year Old, at 43% ABV, is the Lowland bottling of the Classic Malts: vanilla, cut flowers and lemon, soft and gentle.
picks.note: The link to Milton is told with care in the record, as likely and not proven; the Rates are not named in full, as no two sources give their dates. The year a 12 replaced a 10 as the entry bottling is not settled (one shop gives 2007) and is left out. The Kinchie Burn, given here once as the source of the name, was confirmed by no source read and is left out.

picks.why: A distillery on the River Bladnoch near Wigtown in the south west of Scotland, founded by two McClelland brothers in 1817, silent from 2009, bought in July 2015 and distilling again in 2017. The 10 Year Old, bourbon cask malt at 46.7% ABV, not chill filtered and distilled before the silence, is the bottling the roster names; The Spirits Business called it a limited edition at its release, and the producer's range no longer lists it.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: production stopped in 2009 and began again in 2017, so the 10 was distilled before the stop, from the house's own stock; no source says it was bought in. The rankings of retail copy are kept out. Swap refused for now at the c6 read together: the refuter agreed the case for Bladnoch 13 Year Old (the 2024 range of 13 and 16, thirteen years in bourbon casks alone at 46.7% ABV), but the record stands written and refuted for the 10, with the 13 among its others; the flagship moves only when the record is rewritten for the 13 and refuted again, keeping the key and the card ids silence and founding, as reviews/lowland.json sets out.

picks.why: A distillery in the East Neuk of Fife near St Andrews, in a restored farm steading on the Cambo Estate, begun as a golf caddie's idea and opened in November 2014 by the family behind the Wemyss Malts bottling house. Doocot, at 46% ABV, about nine tenths first-fill bourbon barrels and a tenth STR barriques that held Portuguese red wine, from Fife barley malted without peat, is the flagship of a new Lowland that is not only Glasgow and Edinburgh.
picks.note: Not in the style's benchmarks. Settled by the refuted record: Doocot went on sale on 3 March 2023 as the flagship in place of Dream to Dram, which the house retired. The family and the caddie are living and are not named. The family's takeover is told as by 2013 (2012 or 2013 by source). The water source and the barley variety are left out.

picks.why: A distillery beside the ruined abbey of 1191 at Newburgh in Fife, whose first spirit ran in December 2017. The Exchequer Rolls for 1494 record malt given to a friar by order of the king to make aqua vitae, which the distillery ties to the abbey and whisky history tells as the start of its written record in Scotland. MCDXCIV, the year in Roman numerals, is its single malt at 46% ABV, on general sale from 2 July 2021.
picks.note: Not in the style's benchmarks. Settled by the refuted record: the producer titles the bottling Lindores Single Malt Scotch Whisky MCDXCIV, as Wikipedia does; whether the label also prints Lowland was not confirmed. The abbey was founded in 1191, not 1494. The friar is not named, as no source gives his dates, and the 1494 entry is kept as a record, not a first; one account places him elsewhere.

picks.why: A distillery on the south coast of Islay near Port Ellen, set up by two brothers of the Johnston family, officially from 1815, which malts part of its own barley on its floors and dries it over Islay peat, the rest coming from the Port Ellen maltings. The 10 Year Old, ten years in ex-bourbon barrels and 40% ABV as sold in Britain, is the medicinal, peat and seaweed malt that teaches what peat means.
picks.note: Settled in part by the refuted record: 40% ABV stands for the United Kingdom; 43% for the United States rests on shop listings only and is not printed. The floor share is left out (about 10 or 20 per cent by source). The founding brothers are not named in full, as no two sources give their deaths; Ian Hunter (died 1954) and Bessie Williamson (1910 to 1982) are named and dated. The Royal Warrant is left out. Library holds Laphroaig; its 40ppm, its sphagnum peat and its Penicillin measure are not used, for the integrator.

picks.why: A distillery on Lagavulin Bay on the south coast of Islay, dated officially to 1816, when legal distilling began there, on a bay said to have held illicit stills by the 1740s. The 16 Year Old, at 43% ABV and long sold as the Islay malt of the Classic Malts, is deep, slow smoke rounded by age.
picks.note: Peter Mackie (1855 to 1924), who built the White Horse blend on Lagavulin's malt, is named and dated in the record; the year of White Horse (1890 or 1891) is left out. The founder of 1816 is not named, as no two sources give his death. The 16's casks are given by secondary sources as mostly former bourbon with some sherry, against the Library's heavy sherry line, for the integrator. Do not name the 1990s White Horse bottlings as current. Library holds Lagavulin.

picks.why: The third of the south coast Islay distilleries beside Laphroaig and Lagavulin, dated to 1815, closed in 1981 and bought by Glenmorangie in 1997. The Ten, bottled at 46% ABV without chill filtration and introduced in 2000 with the Ardbeg Committee, is heavily peated yet citrus bright, the bottling that shows peat and sweetness together.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the producer names the bottling Ardbeg Ten Years Old, ten years in bourbon casks, non chill-filtered, 46% ABV. Glenmorangie's purchase of 1997, with limited distilling from June 1997 and full output in 1998, stands in Wikipedia and Scotchwhisky.com. The rankings of the producer's own copy are kept out. Library holds Ardbeg; its line on the highest peating is a ranking, for the integrator.

picks.why: The distillery in the island's main town, dated by the house to 1779, which has kept its floor maltings, where part of its barley, given as about 30 to 40 per cent, is turned by hand, and its No. 1 Vaults, partly below sea level on the shore of Loch Indaal. The 12 Year Old, from ex-bourbon and Oloroso sherry casks at 40% ABV, is the middle ground of Islay: smoke with honey and lemon.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the first licensed distillery and the oldest warehouse claims are kept out. The floor share is given as about 30 to 40 per cent, as sources differ; the 25 ppm rests on Wikipedia. 1779 is told as the house's year, with some accounts finding no sure sign of licensed distilling before 1816. The 40% ABV rests on Difford's Guide and shop listings, the producer's page read giving none.

picks.why: A distillery near Port Askaig on the Sound of Islay, founded in 1846 and rebuilt from 1972 to 1974 with six stills in a still house walled in glass, whose malt has long gone mostly into blends, Johnnie Walker among them. The 12 Year Old, at 43% ABV, is a lighter, oily, coastal peat smoke, the Islay malt a guest meets inside blends before they meet it alone.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: 43% on the producer's page. The share kept as single malt is left out (one source). The founder of 1846 is not named, as no two sources give his death; the change of hands of 1852 or 1854 is told only as within a few years.

picks.why: A Campbeltown distillery dated to 1828, which by its own account malts all its own barley on its floors and does every stage on site through to bottling; secondary accounts give the first licence to the Reids, from whom two Mitchell brothers took it over in 1837. The 10 Year Old, lightly peated, distilled two and a half times and bottled at 46% ABV, is the Campbeltown benchmark.
picks.note: Campbeltown has three working distilleries (Springbank, Glen Scotia, Glengyle), so three of this group's five are labels: Longrow and Hazelburn are separately named malts of Springbank distillery and Kilkerran is the malt of Glengyle. Settled by the refuted record: the founding is told as two accounts, the house's (the Mitchells in 1828, on the site of an illicit still) first and the secondary (the Reids' licence of 1828, the Mitchells from 1837) beside it; every stage on site rests on the producer's own distillery page and is hedged as its account, with no claim to be the one distillery to do it; the producer calls the range lightly peated; the 60 and 40 cask split is the 2025 bottling's. Library holds Springbank; its lines on every stage on site as a ranking and on Mitchell ownership since founding are left for the integrator.

picks.why: The second working Campbeltown distillery, founded as Scotia by Stewart, Galbraith and Co in 1832, given the Glen by the Bloch brothers in the 1930s, mothballed in 1984 and bought by Glen Catrine Bonded Warehouse in 1994. Double Cask, first fill bourbon cask malt finished in Pedro Ximenez sherry casks at 46% ABV, is the entry to its range.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the purchase of 1994 by Glen Catrine (Grace's Guide, Scotchwhisky.com) is told and no later owner is named, as the Loch Lomond Group's year is 1996 by its own site and later by others. Victoriana's strength is left out (54.2 or 52.2 per cent by source). The 15 Year Old was offered and declined as flagship: Double Cask opens the producer's core range, and the 15 stands among the record's other bottlings. The Blochs' year is 1930 or 1933 by source, so the record says the 1930s; the finish is up to twelve months by the producer.

picks.why: The malt of Glengyle, the Campbeltown distillery that a company headed by Springbank's then chairman bought in 2000 and brought back into production in 2004 after decades shut; it is sold as Kilkerran because the Glengyle name had passed to another company. The 12 Year Old, first released in 2016, lightly peated, from bourbon and sherry casks at 46% ABV, is its flagship.
picks.note: A label of a distillery with another name: the record says so. Settled by the refuted record: the closure of 1925 stands in the producer's history and Wikipedia, and the dormant years are not counted; the short season worked by the Springbank team is told as the producer's account; the stills came from Ben Wyvis, which closed in the 1970s and was not demolished. The first Kilkerran bottling is 2007 or 2009 by source, so the year field is empty. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Glengyle Distillery (Mitchell's Glengyle).

picks.why: Springbank distillery's heavily peated malt, distilled twice and sold under its own name, so that one distillery makes three malts: Hazelburn unpeated, Springbank lightly peated and Longrow heavily peated. Longrow Peated, with no age statement, from bourbon and sherry casks at 46% ABV, is its standing bottling.
picks.note: A label of Springbank distillery: the record says so plainly. Settled by the refuted record: the producer's page is titled Longrow Peated, at 46% ABV, double distilled; no producer page lists a 10 Year Old as standard, so none is named. The old Longrow warehouse as Springbank's bottling hall and a Penicillin float were cut, for want of a source. Regular distillation is the 1990s by the producer's menu (1990 or 1992 elsewhere). Library holds the distillery as Springbank.

picks.why: Springbank distillery's unpeated malt, from barley dried in the kiln with hot air alone, distilled three times and sold under its own name. The 10 Year Old, ex bourbon cask malt at 46% ABV, shows how far one distillery's spirit moves with peat and the number of distillations.
picks.note: A label of Springbank distillery: the record says so plainly. Settled by the refuted record: the producer calls the 10 Year Old the flagship of the Hazelburn range and bottles it each year at 46% ABV from bourbon casks alone. Hazelburn Sherry Wood is a yearly release whose age changes from one edition to the next. The old distillery's closure is 1925 or 1926 by source, so the record keeps the 1920s. Library holds the distillery as Springbank.

picks.why: A single pot still label first bottled by the Dublin merchants W. and A. Gilbey from Jameson's Bow Street spirit, the making moved to Cork after Bow Street closed in 1971, the name sold to Irish Distillers in 1986 and relaunched as a twelve year old in 1991. Distilled at Midleton from malted and unmalted barley in copper pot stills and matured in former bourbon barrels and sherry butts, bottled at 40% ABV, it is the bottle that shows a guest what Irish pot still tastes like.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the house's heritage page and Wikipedia put the first record of the name in a Gilbey advertisement of August 1912, told as the house's account, and the year field stays empty. The robin story is told as the brand's claim, unnamed, as Wikipedia and Master of Malt also tell it. The producer's 12 page says sherry casks and names oloroso only for the Cask Strength. The Library's Midleton record holds the distillery that makes it; the Library has no Redbreast record of its own. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Midleton Distillery (Irish Distillers).

picks.why: A bonder's label of the Dublin wine merchant Mitchell & Son, named for the daub of paint that once marked the age of a cask in its cellars, a name the house dates to 1925, and made for it at Midleton under an agreement struck when Bow Street closed in 1971. Bottled without an age statement at 40% ABV from pot still whiskey of seven to nine years on average, by the merchant's account, it is the pot still that by the house's account never left the market.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the house dates the name Green Spot to 1925 and its first advertisement to October 1925; that is not shown as a first sale, so the year field stays empty. The average age is seven to nine (Mitchell & Son) or seven to ten (Spot Whiskey), from bourbon and sherry casks. Yellow Spot, Red Spot and Blue Spot are the same label and stay out of every other group; the Ledger's style page names Yellow Spot as a house of its own, for the integrator. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Midleton Distillery, for Mitchell & Son of Dublin.

picks.flagship: Powers John's Lane Release 12 Year Old
picks.why: The Dublin name begun in 1791 by an innkeeper, by the house's account, which traded as John Power & Son by 1822 and whose John's Lane distillery closed within a year or so of the opening of the new Midleton distillery in 1975, when its spirit moved there. John's Lane Release is single pot still aged at least twelve years, mainly in second and third fill bourbon casks with a little oloroso, bottled at 46% ABV without chill filtering: the spicier, oilier Dublin answer to Redbreast.
picks.note: Powers Gold Label, the blend an Irish pub pours, belongs to this same label and is held here; it is kept out of the blended group so that the label is used once. Settled by the refuted record: 1791 stands on the house's story page and in Wikipedia, and the founder is described, not named, for want of his dates; the closure is told as within a year or so of 1975, not 1976; the first fill some accounts give belongs to John's Lane Cask Strength. The year John's Lane Release was first bottled is unsourced. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Midleton Distillery (Irish Distillers).

picks.why: Teeling opened its distillery at Newmarket in Dublin in 2015, and its single pot still, distilled there that year from an even split of malted and unmalted barley and bottled at 46% ABV, came out in October 2018, presented as the first whiskey distilled in Dublin to be bottled in nearly fifty years. It is the bottle that shows pot still from a house outside Midleton.
picks.note: Teeling Small Batch (a blend) and Teeling Single Grain belong to this label and stay here; that is why the Irish single grain group is left. Settled in part by the refuted record: the producer's shop page gives virgin oak, former bourbon and former wine casks and its range page sherry in place of wine; the record tells both, and the label's own words were not read. The family's living members are kept out of prose. The Teeling Whiskey Company's year is 2011 or 2012 by source. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Teeling Whiskey Distillery, Newmarket, Dublin.

picks.why: A distillery in a converted sawmill at Milltown on the edge of Dingle in County Kerry, founded in 2012 by three figures of the craft beer trade, whose first casks were filled in December 2012 and whose first single pot still came in 2017. Its core Single Pot Still, made from local malted and unmalted barley and bottled at 46.5% ABV from September 2025, is the craft counterpoint to the Midleton houses.
picks.note: Dingle stands in the single malt benchmarks too; it is placed here, where its newer core bottling teaches the style, and is kept out of the single malt group. Settled by the refuted record: 46.5% ABV on the producer's shop page and press release; the core and its new look on sale from 18 September 2025. Independence is not told, as it is ownership as a present state, and the first in decades rests on Wikipedia alone and is left out. The co-founder who died in July 2016 is described, not named, as his name stands on people.json's living list, for the integrator to move to historic; the living co-founders are kept out of prose. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Dingle Distillery, County Kerry.

picks.why: The Antrim distillery whose label carries 1608, the year of a royal licence to distil in the district; the distillery company itself was registered in 1784. Its ten year old is triple distilled from malted barley alone and matured mostly in bourbon seasoned barrels with former sherry casks, bottled at 40% ABV: the reference for the soft, triple distilled Irish malt.
picks.note: Tell 1608 as the licence and 1784 as the company, never 1608 as the distillery. Bushmills Original and Black Bush, the blends, belong to this label and are held here, so Bushmills stays out of the blended group. Settled by the refuted record: the house names oloroso only for its cask editions; the 10 to 12 years for the malts in the 10 was met in no source, so the record gives the label's minimum. Aged 10 Years is read only in supermarket listings of the bottle. The Library's oldest licence line is a ranking, for the integrator. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Old Bushmills Distillery, County Antrim.

picks.why: Cooley's peated single malt, first released in 1996, double rather than triple distilled, which, as the house tells it, revives the old Irish habit of drying barley over peat fires. It is the bottle to reach for when a guest asks whether Ireland makes a smoky whiskey.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: 1996 stands in Difford's Guide and Whisky Magazine, and 40% ABV in Wikipedia and Difford's.
