Peat from Scotland rests on a shop alone and is left out, as are the peating level and the share of peated malt; the house names no cask, and the record gives the trade listings' bourbon barrels as theirs. The house's own page calls it Connemara Original; the record keeps the roster's words. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Cooley Distillery, County Louth.

picks.why: A Derry name of the Watt family, whose distillery closed in the 1920s, revived by Cooley Distillery in 1993 or 1994 as a double distilled pot still single malt aged in bourbon casks. Named for a family racehorse, it is Cooley's plain malt to set beside the peated Connemara.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: 1762 and the race's name are left out, and the win of 1876 at a hundred to one is told as the family's story; the closure is 1925 in Difford's and 1921 elsewhere, so the 1920s. The core bottling carries no age statement and is 43% ABV (86 proof) in listings that print the label, earlier bottlings 40%; the producer's own page was not reached. Whether the malt is unpeated was confirmed by no source read, so the record does not say it. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Cooley Distillery, County Louth.

picks.why: A label named for a tower house of 1467 in County Clare, sold as a triple distilled single malt from malted barley, aged twelve years in bourbon casks. It teaches that many Irish malt labels are bottled from another house's stills.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the producer names no distillery, and the record says only that the whiskey is bought in (Difford's, shops and a review name Bushmills, Cooley or Great Northern by period). The house's own pages give both 40% ABV (80 proof) and 43%; the label itself was not read. The bottling is listed current by the house, so it stays. The buyer of 1966 and his wife are described, not named. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Sourced; the triple distillation points to Bushmills.

picks.why: The single malt of Walsh Whiskey, a Carlow house begun in 1999 to blend and bottle an Irish Coffee, triple distilled from Irish barley and aged in bourbon and oloroso sherry casks at 40% ABV. It sits beside Writers' Tears from the same house and shows a malt made to be poured neat.
picks.note: In doubt, as the Library and the style's benchmarks do not name it; it stands, as the house's page shows the bottling current, with no age statement at 40% ABV. Settled by the refuted record: the house names no distillery, so the record says only that the whiskey is bought in (shops say Bushmills, a feature Midleton). The house dates The Irishman to 2006; Writers' Tears is 2008 or 2009 by source. The founders are living and stay out of prose. Dingle, a benchmark of this style, is placed in single pot still instead. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Walsh Whiskey, County Carlow.

picks.why: The name of John Jameson (1740 to 1823), a Scot from Alloa whose Bow Street distillery in Dublin the house dates to 1780; Bow Street fell silent in the early 1970s and the making moved to the new Midleton distillery, opened in 1975. A blend of grain whiskey and single pot still, triple distilled and bottled at 40% ABV, it is the Irish whiskey a guest asks for by name and the usual whiskey of the Irish Coffee.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the house gives June 1970 for the last Bow Street run and others 1971, so the early 1970s; 1780 is told as the house's date, and one account's version (the Stein family founding Bow Street, Jameson its manager and its owner from 1805) as one account; the business traded as John Jameson & Son by 1810. Bow Street 18 is a finish there, not a return of distilling. One house article's Irish pale ale seasoned casks belong to Caskmates and stay out. The Library's Midleton record gives 1825, the old Cork distillery's year, not the new one of 1975: for the integrator. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Midleton Distillery (Irish Distillers).

picks.why: A blend from Tullamore in County Offaly, traced to 1829 and named for the initials of Daniel E. Williams (1848 to 1921), who went to work as a boy in a mill that became part of the distillery and rose to run it as general manager. The Original is a triple blend of grain, malt and pot still whiskey at 40% ABV, and distilling returned to the town when a new distillery opened in 2014.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the town's first distillery is told in the past tense, closed in 1954, and its builders are left out; no claim of being the only blend of its kind is made. The stable boy story was met in no source read, so the record tells the mill. William Grant & Sons bought the brand in 2010 and opened the Clonminch distillery on 17 September 2014. The house's range page gives 40 to 43% by market, the 43% market unnamed; 40% is kept. The Library's stable boy line and its Irish Coffee bar claim are for the integrator. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Tullamore Distillery (William Grant & Sons).

picks.why: A Walsh Whiskey blend with no grain whiskey at all: aged single pot still married to single malt, from malted and unmalted barley, bottled at 40% ABV. It teaches that an Irish blend can be a marriage of the two pot still styles.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the house names no distillery, so the record says the whiskey is bought in and blended; 2009 is the house's year (one account gives 2010), told as its account, and the year field stays empty; triple distilled, unpeated and from flame-charred bourbon barrels by the house's page. Walsh Whiskey was begun in 1999 with a bottled Irish Coffee and bought by Amber Beverage Group in 2021. The Walsh founders are living and stay out of prose. The Irishman, from the same house, is a separate label in the single malt group. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Walsh Whiskey, County Carlow.

picks.why: The Cork Distilleries Company's old Irish whiskey, renamed in the early twentieth century for the salesman who carried it round the pubs of Cork, whose first name the publicans ordered it by. A triple distilled blend of pot still, malt and grain, made at Midleton for Sazerac since a sale agreed in 2016, it is the Cork pour to set beside Jameson.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the renaming is 1912 or 1913 by source, told as the early twentieth century; the salesman worked from 1881 or 1882 until he retired in 1921, and the house and Sazerac name him Patrick J. O'Flaherty, not Paddy Flaherty, but no death year was found, so the record describes him. 40% ABV stands. Sazerac bought Lough Gill Distillery in Sligo in 2022 as a home for Paddy and renamed it Hawk's Rock in 2025; no source read says the making has left Midleton, so madeBy stands and the integrator should watch it. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Midleton Distillery, for the Sazerac Company.

picks.why: Made in the old stables of Slane Castle in County Meath, a distillery Brown-Forman built after buying the brand in 2015, and launched in 2017. It is a blend aged in virgin oak, seasoned American whiskey barrels and oloroso sherry casks, bottled at 40% ABV, and shows a new house teaching cask influence on a blend.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the first Triple Casked was blended from whiskey bought from other Irish distilleries; whether the blend now holds the castle's own whiskey is unsettled, and the record says neither. Brown-Forman bought the brand in 2015 (one source 2016); the distillery opened in 2017 with three pot and six column stills, and Triple Casked came out in May of that year. The castle's family are living and stay out of prose. Powers is held in the single pot still group although its Gold Label is a blend; Bushmills likewise in single malt. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Slane Distillery, County Meath (Brown-Forman).

picks.why: Japan's first malt whisky distillery, begun near Kyoto by Shinjiro Torii in 1923. Suntory brought out Yamazaki as a single malt in 1984, labelled a pure malt at first, and the twelve year old took the words single malt in 2004; at 43% ABV it is the bottle a guest means by Japanese single malt.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: Keizo Saji (1919 to 1999) is named as the founder's son behind the 1984 release; 1923 is the start of building by Suntory's account, and trade sources give 1924 for the opening. Pure malt until 2004 rests on VinePair and trade histories; VinePair's 1986 for the twelve-year age statement and a trade history's Yoichi single malt of 1982 sit against any claim that the 12 was the first single malt Japan marketed, so the record makes none. The label reads The Yamazaki, Single Malt Japanese Whisky, 12 Years Old on the producer's pages. Suntory's living blenders stay out of prose. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Suntory, Yamazaki Distillery.

picks.why: Suntory's second malt distillery, built in 1973 in forest on the slopes of Mount Kaikoma, in the Southern Alps of Yamanashi. Its twelve year old, lightly peated by Suntory's account and herbal at 43% ABV, is the green, mountain counterpoint to Yamazaki.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: 43% ABV; the 43.5% figure was found on one old page only. The peat is told as Suntory tells it, lightly peated, never as a peated whisky; that it varies by batch was found in no source and is left out, as is the altitude of about 700 metres, which rests on one listing. Suntory names no cask for the 12. The pause of 2018 and the return of 2021 rest on news reports. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Suntory, Hakushu Distillery.

picks.why: Nikka's first distillery, built in 1934 on the Hokkaido coast by Masataka Taketsuru, and still distilling over direct coal fire. Its single malt, bottled at 45% ABV, is the heavier, smoky malt every Japanese course sets beside the Suntory pair.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: it teaches the no age statement Nikka Single Malt Yoichi at 45%, which took the place of the age statements withdrawn in 2015; the Yoichi 10 Years Old of 2022 stands in others. The smoke is told as Nikka tells it, from the peat that dried the barley, the coal adding depth. The Important Cultural Property is November 2021 (recommendation) or February 2022 (designation) by source, so the record gives no year and says only that ten buildings stand on the list. Nikka names no casks. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Nikka, Yoichi Distillery.

picks.why: Nikka's second distillery, built in 1969 in the hills of Miyagi, which makes a softer, fruitier malt than Yoichi. Its single malt at 45% ABV lets a guest taste the two Nikka houses side by side.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: it teaches the no age statement Nikka Single Malt Miyagikyo at 45%; the 10 Years Old returned in 2025 in the United Kingdom and in July 2026 in the United States, so it stands in others with no year. The malt stills, by Nikka's own pages, are pot stills with bulging necks and rising lyne arms, heated by indirect steam; the Coffey stills, brought from Scotland in 1963 and first set up at Nishinomiya, were moved to Miyagikyo in 1999 by Nikka's timeline and make grain whisky, not the malt. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Nikka, Miyagikyo Distillery.

picks.why: Hombo Shuzo's distillery in Nagano, founded in 1985 as Mars Shinshu with whisky equipment moved from Yamanashi, silent from 1992 and distilling again from 2011; it took the name Mars Komagatake in 2024. Single Malt Komagatake, made a core bottling at 45% ABV in 2025, shows a Japanese malt house beyond the two large firms.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the producer prints the name as Single Malt KOMAGATAKE, made a core expression on 29 July 2025 at 45% ABV, so no swap; 1985 follows the producer's whisky page (Master of Malt gives 1984). The man who guided Hombo Shuzo into whisky in 1949, once Taketsuru's superior at Settsu Shuzo, is described, not named, for want of a death year in two sources. Mars Whisky as a printed term was not seen on a photograph of the core label. The style page names the house Mars Shinshu, the name before 2024: for the integrator. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Hombo Shuzo, Mars Komagatake Distillery.

groups.title: Japanese blended whisky and the highball

picks.why: Created in 1937 by Shinjiro Torii and named for its square, tortoiseshell cut bottle, a 40% ABV blend drawing on Yamazaki, Hakushu and Chita. It is the whisky of the Kaku Highball, which a Suntory campaign of 2008 brought back to tables across Japan, and the first blend to learn.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the house's own wording is Suntory Whisky Kakubin, and the record uses Kakubin, keeping Kaku for the drink's name; first sold in 1937 simply as Suntory Whisky. Yamazaki and Hakushu malts from bourbon casks sit at the heart of the blend by Suntory's account. The record claims no first for the Kaku Highball: the Ledger's style page dates the Torys highball bars to the 1950s, before the campaign of 2008. Suntory's sales claims stay out, as does the 1937 bottle sold as a twelve year old, on one Suntory page.

picks.why: Suntory's flagship blend, first launched in 1989; Japanese Harmony followed in 2015, a no age statement blend of malt and grain from Yamazaki, Hakushu and Chita at 43% ABV. It is the Hibiki a bar is likely to pour and the lesson in how Japanese blenders build a blend from their own distilleries.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: 43% ABV on Suntory's pages and every listing read; the 42% listing was not found again. Japanese Harmony came out in 2015, about ten malt and grain whiskies from five kinds of cask, American white oak, sherry and Mizunara among them; the fifth kind was named nowhere read, and the month of its American launch differs by source. The aged Hibiki bottlings are not the flagship: the 21 and the 17, paused in 2018, stand in others. The blenders behind Hibiki and Harmony are living and stay out of prose.

picks.why: A Suntory blend made for the highball, built on Hakushu malt and Chita grain with two Yamazaki malts for depth, bottled at 43% ABV with no age statement. Its name means time, and it is the blend a bar keeps on the rail for highballs.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: Suntory's own announcement and Beverage Industry place the launch in the United States in August 2016, so the year field reads 2016, first released. Hakushu malt from American white oak and heavy-type grain from Chita are its two pillars, with Yamazaki malts from American white oak and Spanish oak in support. Its markets after 2016 were not checked. The blender named in Suntory's announcement is living and stays out of prose.

picks.why: A blend of more than a hundred malt and grain whiskies, the malts mostly from Yoichi and Miyagikyo, first released in 1985 in Hokkaido and Aomori and across Japan from 1988, married again in cask and bottled at 51.4% ABV in a small square bottle. It is the Nikka blend a bartender is asked for and shows that a blend can be strong and dense.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the barrel in the name does not mean barrel proof, and the record says so. Nikka's own page says the malts come mostly from its two distilleries; no Scotch malt is named, for want of a primary source. Nikka's own pages, not the label as read, state that it does not meet every criterion of the makers' association standard, and the record puts it there; which criterion it misses Nikka does not say. The bottle's designer and a former chief blender are living and stand in people.json. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Nikka, Yoichi and Miyagikyo.

picks.why: A blended malt, malt whisky only, from Yoichi and Miyagikyo, bottled at 43% ABV and named for Masataka Taketsuru, Nikka's founder. It teaches the other kind of blend: two malts married with no grain.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the record says in its class, table and first trap that this is a blended malt, not a blended whisky. The bottling taught is the no age statement Pure Malt, the one Nikka kept on sale in 2020 when it withdrew the 17, 21 and 25, in a renewed blend; the Taketsuru Pure Malt name dates to 2000. Nikka names key sherry cask malts from both distilleries and gives neither the lead, so no leading malt is named. Whether it meets the makers' association standard is unsettled and unsaid. The benchmarks name Taketsuru under japanese-whisky and japanese-single-malt as an also known; it is placed here.

picks.why: The whisky of Hiram Walker (1816 to 1899), a grocer and grain merchant from Massachusetts who turned to distilling in Detroit in the 1850s and set up his distillery across the river, where the town of Walkerville grew round the works at Windsor; the house dates its beginning to 1858. The 1858 Original, aged in former bourbon barrels and bottled at 40% ABV, is the Canadian whisky a guest names in a highball or a Manhattan.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: no age is given, since the house says only that it ages longer than the three years the law asks and the six years of one retailer stands alone; blending before ageing, the house's old claim, is left out, since a Windsor representative is quoted that it was dropped for the bulk trade; the year Canadian went onto the label (1882, 1889 or 1890 by source) stays out. The record says only where it is made, at the Hiram Walker distillery in Windsor, and never names the company that sells the label. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Hiram Walker & Sons, Windsor, Ontario.

picks.why: Made by Seagram under its president for the royal tour of 1939 by King George VI and Queen Elizabeth, and distilled and blended at Gimli on Lake Winnipeg. Fine De Luxe, a blend the house gives as some fifty whiskies, bottled at 40% ABV, is the Canadian whisky many a guest asks for by its purple bag.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: Gimli's opening year is left out (1968 for the distillery and 1992 for Waterloo's part, one source each); 40% ABV stands on the house's Fine De Luxe page; Seagram's president, Samuel Bronfman (died 1971), is told by his role, his death in one source read; the United States launch is told as the 1960s (1964 in Wikipedia alone). Open for the integrator: whether base whisky also comes from Valleyfield (one review), so the record names Gimli alone; the ten cases on the royal train and the cut-glass bottle are the brand's account. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Crown Royal Distillery, Gimli, Manitoba.

picks.why: The label of the man whose name and initials it carries, who came to Prescott on the St. Lawrence in 1857 to run a distillery, as the house dates it; made at Corbyville after a sale of 1918, its maturing whisky went to Windsor when Corbyville closed in 1989, and it is distilled at Hiram Walker there. Deluxe at 40% ABV is the everyday Canadian blend of Ontario and the bottle that teaches Canadian blending of corn whisky with rye.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: 1857 at Prescott stands on the house's history and Wikipedia, so the year is given; he came to run the distillery, as manager by most accounts and as a partner by one; J.P. Wiser (1825 to 1911) is not named as a person in the record. The sale of 1918 is told as by most accounts (1914, 1920 and 1932 in others), and the move to Corbyville stays undated. No age is given for Deluxe. The company that sells the label is kept out. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Hiram Walker & Sons, Windsor, Ontario.

picks.why: A distillery in Grimsby, between Hamilton and Niagara Falls, opened for fruit brandies in 1972 by the house's account and bought by a winemaker in 1992, whose whiskies of corn, rye and barley are distilled and aged apart and then blended. Barrel Select, first released in 2000 at 40% ABV, is its flagship, and it shows the newer Ontario school beside the older houses of Windsor.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the founder is living and unnamed; the grains are listed without order; the sale of 2014 is left out. Barrel Select's casks are the house's seasoned former bourbon barrels and new white oak; the sherry cask finish three reviews give is not on the house's page, so the record says neither. The Old Pal claim of the first why found no source and is cut. The distillery was Kittling Ridge until it took the name Forty Creek in 2012. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Forty Creek Distillery, Grimsby, Ontario.

picks.why: A rye whisky of rye grain alone by the house's account, distilled in a single copper pot still at Hiram Walker in Windsor, aged in virgin oak and bottled at 43% ABV, named for Lot 40 at Ernestown, a plot where a settler of 1784 kept a grist mill. First released in 1998 and brought back in 2012, it is the rye a bartender reaches for to show what Canadian rye means when it is all rye.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the master blender is living and unnamed; the cask is virgin white oak on Corby's and Pernod Ricard's pages, and the char of the standard bottling was not found. The 2012 recipe is in dispute (90 per cent rye and 10 malted rye in three accounts, all unmalted rye later by the importer alone), so the record gives only the house's 100 per cent. The settler is not named, his death in 1813 standing on one shop page only. Swap refused at the c9 read together: the author's proposed bottling name, Lot No. 40 100% Pot Still Rye Whisky, was refused by the refuter, since the label's words differ by market (Canadian Rye Whisky in US listings, Single Copper Pot Still Canadian Whisky in Ontario, 100% Pot Still Rye Whisky on the house's shop); the roster's name stands, and the integrator may revisit it from a label. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Hiram Walker & Sons, Windsor, Ontario.

picks.why: Taiwan's single malt house in Yilan County, built by the King Car Group after the end of Taiwan's alcohol monopoly and completed in 2005; its first new make ran in March 2006. The Classic, released in December 2008 at 40% ABV, was its first bottling, and it is the bottle that teaches, by the house's account, how heat and humidity quicken maturation.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: 2005 for the building and March 2006 for the first spirit; the day, 11 March, rests on one account and is hedged. The cask make-up, mainly refill and former bourbon barrels with a small share of sherry casks, is the importer's: the house publishes none, so the first why's mainly American oak is cut. 40% ABV in most listings and 43% in the importer's, so no market note. The Cask Atlas chapter names Kavalan already. Made by, as the planner wrote it: King Car Group, Yuanshan, Yilan County, Taiwan.

picks.why: An Indian single malt from Kambipura outside Bengaluru, made from Indian barley of the Himalayan foothills with a smaller share of peated Scottish barley, the two distilled and matured apart and then married, and bottled at 50% ABV. Fusion, first released in 2009, is the bottle that shows how a hot climate gives a young malt depth.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the house gives no barley proportion and accounts differ between a quarter and a fifth, so none is given; six row barley is the Cask Atlas's fact for Paul John, not Amrut, and is cut; no age is given, none standing on the producer's pages; non chill filtering is left out for want of a second source. The family's living members stay out; the founder's son, dead in 2019, is told by his role. Paul John, named in the Cask Atlas chapter, is left out because the label is a living person's name. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Amrut Distilleries, Bengaluru, India.

picks.why: A Melbourne distillery, begun in 2007 in an old hangar at Essendon Fields and moved to Port Melbourne in 2016, whose signature single malt, Nova, is matured entirely in Australian red wine barrels, shiraz and cabernet among them, filled while still wet and bottled at 41% ABV. It is the Australian malt a bar is likely to carry and teaches the wine cask as house style.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the founder is living and unnamed; no source gives Nova an age, so none is given and the two years is cut; the renaming of the Wine Cask release as Nova rests on a review, a blog and a shop, with no year. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Starward Distillery, Melbourne, Australia.

picks.flagship: Sullivans Cove French Oak Single Cask
picks.why: A Tasmanian distillery founded on Hobart's waterfront in 1994, distilling from 1995 and moved to Cambridge outside Hobart in 2004, whose single malts are bottled one cask at a time, at a strength that varies by cask, about 46 to 48% ABV. The French Oak single cask, from casks that held Australian tawny, is the bottle that teaches Tasmanian malt, one cask at a time.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: strength and age are written as varying by cask (46.0 to 48.1% ABV and about nine and a half to eleven years on the house's pages), so the first why's usual 47.5% is cut; award talk stays out; the record tells Tasmania apart from the mainland, as the Cask Atlas asks; Myrtle, the original still, made every run for decades before two more were added in 2023. Swap refused at the c9 read together: the author's proposed bottling name, Sullivans Cove French Oak Ex-Tawny, was refused by the refuter, since French Oak Single Cask is the name the trade lists the bottle under in Australia and the United Kingdom while the house names each release French Oak Ex-Tawny with its cask number; the record carries both, the roster's words in bottle.name and French Oak Ex-Tawny as a label term. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Tasmania Distillery, Hobart.

picks.why: The Welsh distillery in the village of Penderyn, at the edge of the Brecon Beacons, begun as the Welsh Whisky Company in 1998, which first ran spirit from its Faraday still on 14 September 2000 and released its first single malt on St David's Day 2004. Its Madeira Finish, matured in former bourbon barrels and finished in Madeira casks, bottled at 46% ABV, is the house style and the world whisky a British bar is likely to pour beside Scotch.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: Penderyn stays in the group, no swap proposed by the author or made by the refuter, though Wales sits outside the Cask Atlas chapter's four journeys (Taiwan, India, Australia, New Zealand) and the integrator may still prefer Cardrona for New Zealand. The label name is Penderyn Madeira Finish on the producer's product page, at 46% ABV. Jim Swan (died 2017) is named with his death alone, his part hedged as the house's account. The first why's closeness to Scotland was a superlative and is reworded. Made by, as the planner wrote it: Penderyn Distillery, Wales.

picks.why: The Cognac house founded in 1765 by Richard Hennessy (1724 to 1800), an Irish-born officer who had served the French king in the Irish Brigade, whose blenders have come from the Fillioux family since the early 1800s, by its own account. Its V.S carries on the Three Star of the grading by stars the house dates to 1865, and at 40 per cent it is the house's young cognac, poured long or in a Sidecar, and a plain lesson in what the grade letters promise.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the house's international page names it Hennessy Very Special and its American page Hennessy V.S, so bottle.name is Hennessy Very Special Cognac with V.S as a label term; the Library's largest cognac house wording is kept out. The four crus and some forty eaux-de-vie are given as guides give the blend, since the house's V.S pages name neither; the wood is French oak by the house's word, and Limousin is left out. The 1865 star system is told as the house's account, sources crediting a grandson or a great-grandson, so no descendant is named, and the first why's great-grandson is cut; so is its blender buying across the crus, which no source read confirmed. The group is told only as the dated mergers of 1971 and 1987. Open for the integrator: the founder's birth (1724, or 1720 in one genealogy) and his regiment, Clare or Dillon.

picks.why: A Cognac house dated to 1724, founded by a vine grower born near Rouillac, that blends from the Grande and Petite Champagne crus alone. André Renaud (died 1965), who took charge of the house in 1924, launched its VSOP Fine Champagne in 1927, so this one bottle teaches both the VSOP grade and what Fine Champagne means on a label.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the house's own pages give neither the split of the crus nor the ages, so the record gives only the rule of at least half Grande Champagne, as the note asked; the 1724 date is told as the house's founding, never the VSOP's. Renaud is said to have launched the VSOP Fine Champagne, not to have made the first, since sources split between first and popularised; 1938 is the year the Fine Champagne name came into the appellation's law. The group is told only as the merger of 1990 and the name Rémy Cointreau of 1991. Open for the integrator: Renaud at the house from about 1910 in some accounts and 1924 in the house's; the founder is unnamed, his death in one source only.

picks.why: A Cognac house founded in 1715 by Jean Martell (1694 to 1753), a merchant from Jersey. Cordon Bleu, created in 1912 by the founder's great-grandson, is built around a high share of old eaux-de-vie of the Borderies, a small cru, by the house's account, and is the bottling that shows what Borderies brings to a blend.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: Cordon Bleu stays the flagship, the house's named blend since 1912, and the shelf's Martell XO (martell-xo) stands in others and in a trap, so the page and the shelf still meet. Swap not made at the c10 read together: the author offered the XO to the integrator and proposed no swap in form, and the refuter made none. The house calls Cordon Bleu an extra old cognac and the label carries no age statement, so the record claims no XO grade. The Borderies share is told as high by the house's account, the half of one source left out, and the first why's smallest cru is cut as a superlative; Tronçais oak, which the shelf ties to the XO, is not given for Cordon Bleu. Seagram took a share in 1987 and full control in 1988. The great-grandson is unnamed for want of dates.

picks.why: The Cognac house of Jarnac on the Charente, dated by its own account to 1828, when the sons of a Paris wine and spirits firm at Bercy set up a business there that dealt in cognac alone; its tie to Napoléon is the brand's legend of an imperial visit to Bercy in 1811. The VSOP, a blend of four crus with Fins Bois among them, is the round, fruity cognac the house sets in a Sidecar or a Vieux Carré.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: 1828 is the house's date and the record's year (1834, 1835 and 1843 elsewhere for the Jarnac firm); the Napoléon link is told as legend; Campari's purchase from Beam Suntory in 2024 is told as dated history, and no parent is named as present. Louis Renard and a core range of 1909 and 1910 found no source in the author's searches or the refuter's and are cut from the first why; the VSOP is told fruit first, as the house tells it, not cask led. The founding son is not named, his death given as 1866, 1886 or 1873 by source. Open for the integrator: whether the Simon family bought the firm or took its leadership in 1909.

picks.why: A house founded in 1989 as Maison Ferrand to revive the name of a family of Grande Champagne growers at Ségonzac. Its 1840 Original Formula, first released in 2011, was modelled on a Pinet-Castillon cognac of 1840 in the three star style the bartenders of the nineteenth century mixed, and bottled at 45 per cent it is the cognac made for the bar's old classics, the Sidecar, the julep and the punch.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the house's own pages and its new bottle print Ferrand, older labels and the Library Pierre Ferrand, and the record teaches both; the year of the change was not found. The founder of Maison Ferrand, its cellar master and the drinks historian are living and described by role. 45 per cent and Grande Champagne rest on Difford's Guide with a second account; distillation on the lees and the cask type are left out. 2011 rests on Difford's Guide's notes of that year and one review. Jerry Thomas is left out of the record, and now of this why, for want of searched dates. Difford's 1702 for the family is the family's claim and stays out.

picks.why: A family estate near Eauze in the Bas-Armagnac, bought in 1912 by a bear tamer from Ercé and his son, by the estate's account, and passed to the Grassa family through the marriage of the son's daughter; it makes its armagnac only from its own vines, on wood-fired stills of its own since 1985. The VSOP, of Ugni Blanc and Baco, is the estate armagnac a bar can carry and the plain lesson that armagnac is a grower's spirit.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the estate's VSOP sheet gives five to seven years, 60 per cent Ugni Blanc and 40 Baco and 40 per cent, kept apart from the VS Classique's three to five; the estate's 53 to 56 per cent off the still (53 to 54 on its French page) stands in place of the Library's 52 to 60, and the Library's single vintages are not taken up. The first why's Grassa family since 1912 is set right: the Artaud father and son bought the estate that year. Swap refused at the c10 read together: the author's proposed name, Domaine Tariquet, was refused by the refuter, since the estate's 2024 sheets lead with Domaine Tariquet but print SCV Château du Tariquet as the producer line, Difford's Guide and the Library carry the Château name, and no source dates a change; it would also move the pick's producer and its Library link, which is the integrator's. The roster's words stand and a trap teaches both names.

picks.why: A house founded at Condom in 1851 by two partners, one of them a Janneau, which by its own account has aged its armagnac in the cellars built that year ever since, and which by the same account won back the right to double distil in pot stills in 1972. The VSOP, at 40 per cent, blends spirit of both stills, is a common first armagnac on a back bar, and the Atlas chapter already names the house.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the house is never called the oldest; no age beyond VSOP is given, the house saying only that some eaux-de-vie in the blend have up to twenty years in French oak; the VSOP blends spirit of the continuous still with spirit double distilled in Charentais pot stills. The founder is not named for want of dates, so the first why's Pierre Etienne Janneau is cut, and the 1851 cellars are told as the house's account; the sale to Martell is dated 1974 as the house gives it, and the owners after are left out. Open for the integrator: the year the pot still was barred, 1903 by the house and 1936 or 1943 elsewhere, is told as the house's; Difford's Guide gives 7 to 12 years, mostly in Limousin oak, against the house's twenty in French oak.

picks.why: An estate at Sorbets in the Bas-Armagnac, dating from 1870 and bought by the Lesgourgues family in 1974, that grows and distils all four of the grapes an armagnac label names, Baco, Colombard, Folle Blanche and Ugni Blanc, each variety apart on its own still, and coopers its own casks of Gascon oak. The VSOP shows what a whole estate's grapes give in one blend.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: 1870 stands on the estate's pages, its importer and Difford's Guide as the founding, not the year a building went up, and no source gives 1855; the estate's size and the single block of the first why (one shop's page) are left out. The family's present generation is living and unnamed. The three-year drying of the staves found no source and is cut; the cooperage of Gascon oak is told as Difford's Guide's and the importer's, and its claim to be the only one is left out. Open for the integrator: the VSOP's grape shares are unpublished.

picks.why: One of the two names under which the Delord family of Lannepax sells its armagnac. The house dates its story to 1893, when its founder, a travelling distiller, married into the Duffau family; his sons set up Delord Frères, and the importer gives 1925 as the company's founding. The Napoléon, no eau-de-vie in it younger than six years, at 40 per cent, is a Bas-Armagnac a guest may well have met in a shop.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the pick is the label and Delord makes it, so Delord stays an alternate only. The house's own pages date the story to 1893 and speak of the founder and his two sons but never of Marie Duffau; the link rests on the importer and Wikidata, and the name is told as a forebear's, since the importer's two accounts differ between the founder's wife and a great-grandmother. The first why's Marie Duffau as a founder with her husband and son, and its two names since 1925, are the importer's account and are set right. The founders are not named for want of dates. Open for the integrator: the importer's 1925 with the founder, his wife and a son against the house's two sons; the grape shares rest on the importer.

picks.why: An armagnac house at Roquefort in the Landes, founded in 1974 by the son of a restaurant family of Villeneuve-de-Marsan, that chooses and ages casks from about thirty Bas-Armagnac estates. Les Grands Assemblages are its blends by age, set beside its single-estate vintages, so the 20 Ans, at 43 per cent, teaches how an armagnac éleveur works.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the house's present head is living and described by role; 43 per cent stands on the house's page and listings, the 40 per cent listings not seen again; Roquefort is confirmed by the house's company name and Difford's Guide. Distilling at fifteen estates found no source and is cut; the single-estate pages show continuous distillation. The single-estate range's own name carries a refused word, so the record and now this why describe it without naming it. Open for the integrator: the son joined in 1994 by the house and 1996 in one account; the 20 Ans grapes are Baco and Ugni Blanc by the house, with shares unpublished.

picks.why: A family house of the Pays d'Auge, begun in 1960 when a farm of cider apple orchards at Gonneville near Honfleur came to its founder; it first sold its calvados in 1979 and moved to Coudray-Rabut in the early 1990s, and its Pays d'Auge range is double distilled in pot stills. Its young Sélection, column distilled AOC Calvados from apples and pears, is the calvados a bar uses for the Widow's Kiss and the Corpse Reviver No. 1.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the Sélection does not read Calvados Pays d'Auge; it is AOC Calvados, column distilled from cider and perry and aged in old casks, so the first why's pot stills belong to the Pays d'Auge range alone, and Sélection is no age mention, so only the appellation's two years are given. The house dates from 1960, when the farm came to the founder (no source gives a purchase), and first sold in 1979, which is why some accounts give about 1980; a trap says so. The family's generations are living or share a living name, and none is named. Open for the integrator: whether newer stock reads Christian Drouin, Drouin or C. Drouin was not read off a bottle.

picks.why: A Pont-l'Évêque house dating itself to 1821, its distillery and cellars on the road out of the town towards Trouville, where its old cellars opened to visitors as the Calvados Experience in 2018. Its VSOP is a Calvados Pays d'Auge of at least four years, double distilled as the appellation requires, at 40 per cent, and a calvados a guest will often have seen in a shop.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: owners are left out; the Pays d'Auge wording stands for the British and European bottle, while an American listing names it only VSOP Calvados and no American label was read, so the owner should check the bottle in hand. The innkeeper of the name rests on one retailer and is cut from the first why. The VSOP's double distillation is told from the appellation's rule; the VS Fine is plain AOC Calvados. Open for the integrator: a Fine Pays d'Auge listed by one British shop beside the VS Fine.

picks.why: A house of the Pays d'Auge founded in 1825, which by its own account double distilled from the start and pressed for the Pays d'Auge appellation of 1942, and which distils at the Moulin de la Foulonnerie at Coquainvilliers. Its VSOP blends Pays d'Auge calvados of at least four years, double distilled in pot stills and married again in cask, and shows the appellation's ripe apple fruit.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the family's hand in the 1942 appellation is told as the house's claim, in the story and a trap; the four to ten years of the first why is the importer's and is cut, the house giving at least four. The founder is not named for want of dates, and the present head is living and unnamed. A sale of 2007 to Spirit France rests on retailers and an interview and stays out of the record, so the first why's still in his family is cut. Open for the integrator: one merchant founds the house at Yvetot.

picks.why: The calvados bottled under Maison Ferrand, the Cognac house founded in 1989: a young Pays d'Auge at 40 per cent, of bitter and bittersweet apples with pears, double distilled in small Charentais pot stills and aged in small used Limousin oak, by Ferrand's page. It is a Pays d'Auge made with the shaker in mind, from a house that builds bottlings for bartenders.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: where Daron is distilled is not said; the Charentais pot stills and the Limousin oak now stand on Ferrand's own page for Daron with Difford's Guide, and the orchards north of the Pays d'Auge rest on one source and stay out. No age is given beyond the appellation's two years, the about five years of the first why resting on Difford's Guide and shops. The owner's fall menu prints Daron Fin Calvados, and the record follows Ferrand's spelling, Fine. Maison Ferrand also makes the Ferrand cognac pick; the labels are separate. Open for the integrator: whether Fine is a listed age mention of the current rules.

picks.why: A family estate at the Clos de la Hurvanière, Saint-Cyr-du-Ronceray, in the Pays d'Auge, where by the estate's account Pierre Groult (1830 to 1918) began distilling his own cider in 1860, and which double distils in antique copper pot stills over a wood fire. The Réserve 3 Ans, all apple and at least three years in old oak, is the estate's young calvados and a clear lesson in how fresh apple reads after three years.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the eighteenth century of the first why is in neither the estate's history nor Wikipedia (1860, or about 1850) and is cut, and year stays empty. The dead of the family are named with their dates; the present generation is living and unnamed. The group shows the broad appellation once after all, since the Christian Drouin Sélection is plain AOC Calvados; the pear led Domfrontais has no pick, and Le Domfrontais stands in that record's others. Swap refused at the c10 read together: the author's proposed bottling, Roger Groult Calvados Pays d'Auge 3 Ans d'Âge, was refused by the refuter, since the estate prints both names (3 ans d'âge on its shop page, Reserve 3 years old on its cocktail page) and shops in several markets list Réserve 3 Ans; the roster's words stand and a trap teaches both names.

swaps.why: The cooperative makes two Reservado bottlings at 40 per cent; the clear Transparente, in steel, is the record's and its own page's name, and the record was written for it and refuted.

picks.why: The pisco of Hacienda La Caravedo in Ica, a distillery that dates its own distilling to 1684. Its Mosto Verde is made in single grapes and as an acholado; the record names the Acholado, a blend of Quebranta, Torontel and Albilla, distilled once from must whose fermentation has not finished, and it teaches Peru's rule that pisco goes into the bottle at the strength it came off the still.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: 43 per cent stands on the distillery's page; its master distiller is living, described by role and in people.json; the Portón registration in the United States was cancelled in 2017 and the distillery's piscos sell there as Caravedo, taught in a card, a trap and others. The bottling swap to Caravedo Mosto Verde, proposed on condition, was refused by the refuter: the owner's market is not known, the distillery's Peruvian pages print Pisco Portón, and the change would rename the label, not only the bottling; the owner may still ask for it. Open: the year Caravedo reached American shelves, the still and the brand's first release.

picks.why: A Peruvian pisco distilled once in copper pot stills at Bodega San Isidro in Ica, a bodega idle since 1968 and brought back to work in 2002 by a group of investors based in the United States. Primero Quebranta is pure Quebranta, the non aromatic grape that gives pisco its body, bottled at 41.3 per cent with no water added.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the bodega's founding stays out (a century old by the house, 1919 in the town's archive, the building likely of the 1800s); the buyers of 2002 and the master distiller are living, described by role and in people.json. The bottling swap to BarSol Puro Quebranta Pisco, the name the house, its importer and a release of July 2026 print, was refused by the refuter for now: the record is written and refuted for the roster's Primero, which shops in several markets still print, and teaches Puro Quebranta in others and the story; a swap wants bottle.name rewritten and refuted with it.

picks.why: A Peruvian pisco founded in 2006 by two sisters, its plain bottling Quebranta alone, distilled once in copper pot stills in the Ica valley and rested a year, by the house's account, before bottling at 40 per cent. It is a Quebranta pisco for the Pisco Sour, and its acholado and mosto verde, La Diablada and Ñusta, show Peru's other two styles.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the sisters are living, named nowhere and in people.json under both surnames the sources give; no distillery is named, since the house's pages name none and the Tacama claim rests on one shop. Open: 40 per cent (80 proof) stands on three sources, against 44 from Canada's provincial board and about 42 for the distillate in Difford's Guide, and no label was read.

picks.why: The pisco of a growers' cooperative of the Elqui Valley, founded at Paihuano in February 1938 by twenty-five growers and given its legal standing in 1939, its name the initials of Cooperativa Agrícola Pisquera Elqui; it later bought the distillery at Vicuña that became its plant. Its Doble Destilado Reservado Transparente, Pedro Jiménez distilled twice and rested a year in steel at 40 per cent, is the clear pisco for a Piscola and teaches that Chile grades pisco by strength, not by age.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the cooperative makes two Reservado bottlings at 40 per cent, the clear Transparente rested in steel and the Reservado de Guarda rested six to eight months in American oak, so the flagship was swapped to the Transparente; 1938 stands on the cooperative's own history; Chile's grades by strength are Decree 521 of 1999, from 30 per cent for Corriente to 43 for Gran Pisco, and Peru's rules are kept off the page. Open: the year the Vicuña plant was bought and the year the name Capel was first used; the taste rests on tasters, the cooperative giving no note.

picks.why: The Chilean pisco of Miguel Torres Chile, the house the Torres family of Penedès founded in the Curicó Valley in 1979, made by the house's account from 2012 of Moscatel of Alexandria and pink Moscatel from the Limarí Valley, distilled once in copper and rested in steel. At 40 per cent, the Reservado grade, it is the pisco on the owner's shelf and a clear lesson in an aromatic, muscat led Chilean pisco.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: 2012 stays the house's account and out of the year field, for want of an independent date; the family member who created it is living and named nowhere. The governor, who fought at Maipú in 1818 and later governed Ovalle, is described and not named, since his dates were found nowhere. For the integrator: the liquor shelf's El Gobernador record names him without dates and says Reservado means 40% ABV, where the decree makes 40 the minimum, below Gran Pisco at 43.

swaps.why: The American label and the importer's page name the bottling Fundador Sherry Cask Solera Reserva; the refuter rewrote the record for it.

swaps.to: Cardenal Mendoza Clásico Solera Gran Reserva
swaps.why: The bodega sells this bottling as Cardenal Mendoza Clásico, beside its older Carta Real and Non Plus Ultra; the record was written for it and refuted.

picks.why: The brandy the Domecq house of Jerez first sold under the name Fundador in 1874, by the brand's account, and which the house calls the first Brandy de Jerez. The Sherry Cask Solera Reserva, aged by criaderas and solera in American oak casks that held sherry to an average of at least one year, is the young brandy a guest names when he asks for Spanish brandy.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the American label and the importer's page print Sherry Cask Solera Reserva, so the flagship was swapped to that form; Emperador completed its purchase of Bodegas Fundador from Beam Suntory in 2016, the González Byass pages being the American importer's, and madeBy names the bodega only; the founder is described for want of his dates; two living names of Emperador are in people.json. Open: where the brandy is distilled, and the Spanish Fundador Solera's 36 per cent, no longer stated.

picks.flagship: Cardenal Mendoza Clásico Solera Gran Reserva
picks.why: The Solera Gran Reserva of Sánchez Romate in Jerez, made by the house's account from 1887 by the family's fourth generation, named for Cardinal Pedro González de Mendoza (died 1495) and sold as Clásico beside the older Carta Real. The bodega gives it an average of fifteen years in American oak seasoned with oloroso and Pedro Ximénez, and it is the old Brandy de Jerez a bar keeps for the guest who wants a Spanish brandy after dinner.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the fifteen year average stands on the bodega's own sheet; the council's floor for Solera Gran Reserva is an average of three years, not ten, by its own page and specification (one year for Solera Reserva, six months for Solera); the bodega sells the bottling as Clásico, so the flagship was swapped to that form. Open: Carta Real's age (over 25 or about 30 years by source) stays out; the founder of 1781 stays described.

picks.why: González Byass's senior brandy, launched in 1951 by the house's account and distilled twice from Palomino wine in two Charentais copper pot stills at its Los Arcos bodega in Jerez, which the house says makes it a brandy made wholly in Jerez. The Solera Gran Reserva ages about twelve years by criaderas and solera, nine in casks that held Tío Pepe fino and three in casks that held Matusalem oloroso.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: made wholly in Jerez is told as the house's description, and no count of the brandies distilled in the town was found, so neither the only one nor one of the few is written; twelve years stands on the bodega's sheet; 36 per cent is the bodega's for Europe, and 40 for the United States rests on one retailer and the 80 proof floor of 27 CFR 5.145. The stills of the 1960s and the battle behind the name stay out.

picks.why: Osborne's Solera Gran Reserva, a brand that dates its solera to 1889 and that Osborne bought from Pernod Ricard España in 2008, by the competition authority's file. Osborne's report of 2020 gives a solera of sixteen scales of American oak casks that held sherry and an average of twelve years, with vanilla and cocoa from the wood, and it is a Brandy de Jerez a guest from Spain will often ask for by name.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: twelve years and sixteen scales stand on Osborne's report of 2020, and 40 per cent on the Spanish trade sheet and one listing; Osborne's 1772 is told as the year of the Cádiz partnership its founder later joined; the Imperial XO and the 1520 are separate bottlings, in others. Open: the brand's descent from the Pedro Domecq house rests on one writer and stays out, as do the name's tie to the emperor and the bodega where the solera is kept.

picks.flagship: Gran Duque d'Alba Solera Gran Reserva
picks.why: A Brandy de Jerez first made in 1945 by Williams & Humbert, the Jerez house two British partners founded in 1877, and named for the third Duke of Alba, the sixteenth century general, at the suggestion of the duke of the day. Made from young Palomino and Airén wines, distilled in pot stills and aged by criaderas and solera in American oak casks that held oloroso, twelve years on average by the bodega, it is the dark, raisined Gran Reserva to set beside Cardenal Mendoza.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the bodega's pages give twelve years on one and ten on another, and a trap teaches both; an American importer lists the brandy, but none is named, since that can change; no owner is named. Open: the founders and the dukes stay described for want of dates in two sources; where the wine is distilled and the XO's age stay out; the house prints de Alba where its importer prints d'Alba. This group is thinner at an American bar than cognac: Fundador and Cardenal Mendoza are met often, the other three mostly where a bar has a Spanish list.

picks.flagship: Laird's Straight Apple Brandy Bottled in Bond
picks.why: The apple brandy of Laird & Company, a New Jersey family firm based at Scobeyville that dates itself to 1780, the first commercial sale in its records, and whose distilling has all taken place at North Garden, Virginia, since 1976. The bonded straight apple brandy, apple alone with no neutral spirit, at least four years in charred oak as the bond law requires and 100 proof, is the bottle for a Jack Rose.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: four years stands on the house and 27 CFR 5.88, and Difford's three is taught as a trap; 1780 is the house's own, and the claim to be the oldest licensed distillery is left out; North Garden since 1976 is on the house's history page; the applejack lesson is Laird's Applejack, the federal blended class with neutral grain spirit at 80 proof, beside the bonded apple brandy and Straight Applejack 86. A living member of the family is in people.json. Open: the still, the bottling place, the year of the blended applejack class (1968 or 1972) and whether a Laird served under Washington or supplied his troops.

picks.why: The California brandy of E. & J. Gallo, first bottled in March 1975 after five years of trials at the company's Fresno distillery, by its own account, and named for the brothers Ernest and Julio Gallo. The VSOP, sold as E&J VSOP Grand Blue and given at least two years in oak by the brand, not Cognac's four, pours brown spice, vanilla cream and maple, and is the bottling to know.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the VSOP stays the flagship, sold as E&J VSOP Grand Blue, which carries every word of the roster's; many bars pour the VS as the well brandy, and a swap to it stays open to the owner, none proposed; the brothers are named with their dates (Ernest 1909 to 2007, Julio 1910 to 1993); no ranking or sales figure is given; living members of the family are in people.json. Open: the type of still.

picks.why: A grape brandy with a California past: the brand dates itself to 1882 and the De La Salle Brothers' winemaking at Martinez, its first brandy came in 1940, the order sold the business in 1989, and Heaven Hill bought it with the Bernheim Distillery in 1999. The VS rests at least two years in former bourbon barrels and is bottled at Bardstown, Kentucky, the plain example of grape spirit from the West rested in bourbon wood.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: Heaven Hill makes it, by its own brands page and history; the brand's 1882 is set against the 1940 that the brand's history and the Mont La Salle marker give for the first brandy; the order sold to Heublein in 1989; Heaven Hill and the brand's site write Christian Brothers without The, while the roster and older labels carry it. Open: where and on what still the VS is distilled, whether European brandy is in the blend, and whether the front label reads VS for Very Smooth; no front label was read.

picks.why: The brandy of Korbel, the Russian River sparkling wine house at Guerneville dated to 1882, which installed its first still in 1889 by its own account. The California Brandy, French Colombard and Chenin Blanc distilled on a copper-lined continuous column, aged at least two years in charred American oak and blended through a solera, is the brandy Wisconsin has long built its Brandy Old Fashioned on.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the still, the grapes, the oak and the solera are the house's; the Chicago fair of 1893 as the birth of Wisconsin's Brandy Old Fashioned is told as a legend; the Brown-Forman barrels and sales found no source and stay out; the founding brothers and the buyers of 1954 are described, one of that family being living and in people.json. Open: the taste has no producer's note.

picks.why: A brandy distillery opened in the Butchertown district of Louisville in 2014, with copper pot stills and brandy rested in Kentucky bourbon barrels; distilling went on there after its sale to a Louisville firm in 2025. The American Craft Brandy, at 90 proof, blends the house's own pot still brandy with pot still brandy bought from other distillers, and is the pot still American brandy a bartender should know beside the big California houses.
picks.note: Settled by the refuted record: the distillery has not closed; Constellation Brands took a minority stake in 2018 and the rest in 2020, and the Bourdon Spirits Company of Louisville bought it in August 2025, all told as dated history; the founders are living, described and in people.json. The bottling swap to Copper & Kings American Brandy V.S.O.P. was refused by the refuter for now: the house no longer lists a 90 proof American Craft Brandy, but the V.S.O.P. is another spirit (six years, the house's own distillate, 86 proof) that wants its own record researched and refuted before the flagship moves; until then the record teaches the American Craft Brandy as it was sold. Open: the grapes rest on Distiller and shops, the house saying only American wine.

left.why: Thin. The four grain bourbons a guest might meet are Rabbit Hole Cavehill (the shelf bottle, rabbit-hole-cavehill), Penelope and a handful of craft bottlings (Black Button, Bluebird, A.D. Laws) that few bars carry by name; Woodford Reserve's Four Grain was a single Master's Collection release of 2005 and Balcones is a corn and malt house. Fewer than five real labels a working bar is asked for, so no group. If the merge agent wants one, Rabbit Hole would have to move here with Cavehill, and Rabbit Hole Heigold leave high-rye.

A label term, not a kind of producer. Straight qualifies bourbon, rye, wheat and corn whiskey, and the bottlings a bartender is asked for by name carry it as bourbon or rye, not as their identity; no five labels sell themselves as straight whiskey alone. It is taught through the rye, corn and bourbon groups (Rittenhouse, Pikesville, Old Overholt, Mellow Corn all print straight).

Thin. Only three labels a guest would meet are wheat whiskey first: Bernheim Original (Heaven Hill, seven years, 90 proof, 51 wheat, released 2005), Dry Fly (Spokane, Washington wheat) and Middle West. Woodford Reserve Wheat and Old Elk Wheat are real but come from labels that are first bourbon labels, and the Weller and Stitzel-Weller names in the prose are wheated bourbons. Fewer than five, so no group: Bernheim Original is the one bottle to teach the style.

Thin as a style a guest names. Seagram's 7 Crown (Diageo, 80 proof, about 75 per cent neutral grain spirit) and Kessler (founded 1888, Smooth as Silk, now Suntory Global Spirits, 80 proof) are asked for by name; Fleischmann's Preferred (Sazerac Company, 80 proof) is a rail bottle; Imperial and Calvert Extra are still listed but nothing more could be confirmed. High West, on the benchmarks, sells blends of straight whiskeys, not blended American whiskey with neutral spirit, so it is not of the style. No light whiskey label is in general sale. Two real names and three rail blends do not make five a bartender is expected to know; teach Seagram's 7 Crown and Kessler in the style's own prose.

A category, not a kind of producer: every single malt in this lane belongs to it, and its groups are the six regions (Speyside, Highland, the Islands, Lowland, Islay, Campbeltown), so a separate group of five would only repeat their picks.

The Lowland benchmarks list names Cameronbridge, which is a grain distillery and not a malt house, and Rosebank, which closed in 1993 and only resumed distilling in 2023 with no core bottling yet; neither is picked, and the author may wish to correct the list. Kingsbarns and Lindores Abbey are picked in their place.
Campbeltown has three working distilleries and every label they make is either picked or offered; both alternates are therefore other bottlings of Glen Scotia, not sixth and seventh houses.

Left by the merge: the group cannot reach five without padding. Its own lane says only Haig Club is a label a guest asks for on the rail, that Cameron Brig is of uncertain supply and may be told as history, and that RyeLaw and Arbikie, specialist bottles, fill the five; of its alternates, The Girvan Patent Still shows no release since 2014 and The Sovereign has no one fixed bottling. The lane's five picks and two alternates stay in plan-lanes/scotch-categories.json should the owner want the group after all. Until then the style is taught on its own page.

The fifth category of the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 (grain whiskies of more than one distillery, for example Compass Box Hedonism) has no row in the styles roster, so it was judged and left; it belongs in the single grain style text, not as a group.

The group is made, but thin: only Haig Club is a label a guest asks for on the rail. Cameron Brig is of uncertain current supply, Girvan Patent Still shows no release since 2014, and the grain plants the benchmarks name (Girvan, North British, Invergordon) sell almost nothing under their own names, so RyeLaw and Arbikie, specialist bottles, fill the five. The author should judge whether to teach the last two as the new face of the style.

Thin, and the one name a guest asks for is already used. The real single grain labels found are Teeling Single Grain (Cooley grain, red wine casks, 46% ABV), Kilbeggan Single Grain (made at Cooley, mostly corn, 43% ABV), Method and Madness Single Grain (Midleton, 46% ABV) and Glendalough Double Barrel (Coffey still, 42% ABV), with The Busker as a possible fifth. Teeling stands in single pot still and Kilbeggan in its alternates, so the group would be three or four labels of bottlings few guests ask for by name. Teach the style through the label term on its own page.

A standard, not a kind of producer: the makers' association rule of 2021 (malted grain and Japanese water, distilled, aged at least three years and bottled in Japan) covers malts, grain and blends alike. Its houses are carried by japanese-single-malt and japanese-blended.

A wood, not a kind of producer. No five bottlings are asked for by name with Mizunara as their identity; the benchmarks (Yamazaki, Chivas Regal, Bowmore) use it as a finish or a limited release. Teach it on its page through those houses.
Five labels a guest asks for by name do not exist: Laird's is the applejack a bar carries and the others are small local apple brandies. Applejack is taught through Laird's inside American brandy.

No brandy style exists in tools/caskstyles/plan.json, so every group here has style "": cognac, armagnac and calvados hang on their Cask Atlas chapters, and pisco, Brandy de Jerez and American brandy have neither a chapter nor a style yet.
